units.title: Starkenn shows 2,500+ vehicles. Are we not already behind?
units.body: The number does not survive its own source. The single Nov-2024 interview it comes from also says ‘over 700 units sold’ and ‘300+ vehicles have deployed our tech’ — three figures for one quantity, self-reported and unaudited, now ~21 months old. Starkenn is a 57-person company shrinking 15.8% year on year on $2.0m of lifetime funding. What is real is its 30% government-tender share and 40% subscription revenue — empanelment and recurring revenue, not scale. units.title: The ASIC gives us a 3–7× cost advantage. Why gate the capital?

units.title: Why only four gates? Can we not run more in parallel?
units.body: Four parallel gates already exceed the engineering and management capacity of a company this size. Running six dilutes all of them rather than clearing any one. The stop rule is explicit: re-plan if two of four miss their first milestone.

units.body: DeepGrid cannot win India CV ADAS as a full-system supplier — ZF and Aptiv own braking, ECU, calibration, approval and warranty. units.title: Four contests to lose deliberately
units.body: The dossier says where to compete. It never says where to stop — so every arena stays notionally open and scarce evidence spend gets spread across all of them. Each is falsifiable: the trigger column states what would reopen it. · 1 Jan 2027 line-fit · UNWINNABLE ON TIME · Design-in for an OEM programme runs 18–30 months. It is August 2026. A programme binding 1 Jan 2027 was specified before DeepGrid could have entered it. · Reopen only if an OEM offers a mid-cycle perception swap with no re-homologation. · Full-system AEBS supply · STRUCTURALLY CLOSED · Rule 96(12) obliges a system that brakes. The safety case, calibration and warranty sit with the actuator owner, and ZF will not hand those over. · Reopen only if a braking Tier-1 offers a white-label safety case — which none has ever done. · Warning-only retrofit on price · ADVANTAGE IS WORTHLESS HERE · drivebuddyAI, bitsensing and Starkenn already hold it, and it requires no certification at all — so the functional-safety pathway DeepGrid must still ACQUIRE would buy nothing here even once it exists. units.title: The one holding the seat owns no silicon at all
units.body: DeepGrid's thesis is owned silicon. Mapping who actually depends on whom tests that thesis directly — and the answer is uncomfortable. Two of the three companies that reach brake actuation buy their perception rather than build it, and the company occupying the exact seat DeepGrid wants owns no silicon whatsoever. Meanwhile the two players with the most credible silicon story — Gahan and Netrasemi — have no route to an Indian CV buyer between them. On this evidence, silicon ownership is neither necessary nor sufficient to hold the perception seat. It is a margin and supply-assurance argument, not an entry argument, and the deck should stop selling it as one. · STRADVISION · None — hardware-agnostic · Runs on whatever the integrator chooses; designed for low-cost constrained hardware · HOLDS THE SEAT · EV-SV-03 · Aptiv · Own Gen 8 radar + Gen 7 camera · But the perception INSIDE the camera is STRADVISION's, not Aptiv's · OWNS THE PLATFORM · EV-APT-02 · ZF · Own OnGuardMAX + short-range radar · Owns the actuator, so the silicon question never decides the sale · OWNS THE SAFETY CASE · EV-ZF-02 · Gahan AI · TI AWR2944 · AEC-Q100 attaches to TI's IC; TI's own CES release names no Indian partner · NO ROUTE TO MARKET · EV-GHN-02, EV-GHN-04 · Netrasemi · TSMC 12nm, own NPU/VPU/ISP · Real Indian silicon — with no AIS, AEC-Q100 or ISO 26262 · NO CERTIFICATION · EV-NTR-02 · bitsensing · N

units.title: Four rivals keep earning after the sale. DeepGrid stops at the invoice.
units.body: A module vendor ships once. Every competitor below holds a channel to the vehicle after start of production — which is where the customer relationship actually lives. OTA is the underrated threat on this list. It converts ADAS from a shipped part into a maintained service: the incumbent's field performance improves after SOP, and the customer relationship stays with the integrator. A merchant module vendor cannot answer that with a better die. units.title: Aptiv's win and STRADVISION's win may be the same programme
units.body: The dossier counts these as two competitive events. The evidence does not establish that they are. If it is one programme, the field has one Indian CV line-fit win between Aptiv and STRADVISION, not two, and the dossier overstates the pace of competitive capture. If it is two, then STRADVISION is selling into India independently of Aptiv as well as inside it, which makes it a broader threat than the profile allows. Both readings change a rating. Neither is established, and the honest move is to carry the question rather than pick the flattering answer. UNRESOLVED — do not merge, do not double-count

units.title: One of these nine is a competitor. The other eight are something else.
units.body: Threat rating asks how dangerous a company is. It presumes the company is bidding for the same thing — and by the dossier's own obstruction scores, six of nine are not. Pattern first, rating second. Six of the nine score 2/5 or less on obstructing the position DeepGrid has chosen, and the dossier says so in its own words — 'blocks nothing', 'no overlap', 'a partner-shaped competitor'. A threat ranking across all nine therefore compares things that were never comparable, and it spends the scarce evidence budget on companies DeepGrid will never bid against. The pattern determines the verb: displace one, sell to three, ignore three for the mandate, out-argue two. · SUBSTITUTE · Sells the same thing to the same buyer for the same job. Interchangeable at the point of decision. · STRADVISION · 5/5 · Displace or differentiate. This is the only company where 'win the deal' is the right verb. · Porter — rivalry · EV-SV-01, EV-SV-03, EV-SV-05 · GATEKEEPER · Does not sell what you sell. Decides who gets to. · Aptiv · 4/5 · Sell TO, not against. The buying decision you must win is its vendor-selection, not an end customer's. · Value Net — customer · EV-APT-01, EV-APT-02 · CHANNEL / COOPETITOR · Owns a control point you must pass through, and is simultaneously your route to market. · ZF · Sterling × MINIEYE · 3/5 · 1/5 · Attach. units.title: The same company can be a customer and a rival at once
units.body: Brandenburger & Nalebuff's Value Net places four roles around a firm. The dossier collapsed all four into one axis called threat — which is why ZF, a company DeepGrid intends to sell through, was ranked as an adversary. Three companies sit in two quadrants at once. ZF and Aptiv are customers today and become competitors only if they in-source the perception layer — which is precisely the counter-move page's finding, and precisely why the counter-move risk and the blocker rank disagree. units.title: The dossier is a market map wearing a competitor dossier's clothes
units.body: Applying the patterns changes what each page is for, and where the evidence budget should go. None of this says the research was wasted. The evidence stands and the ratings are sound within their rows. What changes is the shape: a dossier that treats a route-to-market as an adversary will keep producing plans to out-compete the companies DeepGrid most needs to sell to, and will keep under-investing in the single displacement contest that actually decides the strategy. · What the dossier does now · What the pattern says it should do · Nine competitor profiles, equally weighted, each with a threat rating · ONE competitor to beat (STRADVISION), THREE accounts to win (Aptiv, ZF, Sterling), THREE markets to note and leave, TWO narratives to counter · A threat heatmap spanning all nine across three arenas · A relationship map: substitute · gatekeeper · channel · different job · narrative · supplier. units.title: Sell the braking Tier-1 the object list its safety case needs — never the brake decision
units.body: Rule 96(12) obliges AEBS plus Vehicle Stability Function on M2/M3/N2/N3 from 1 Jan 2027. The system must warn at least 1.4 s before it brakes and may not enter the emergency phase before TTC 3.0 s. That budget is a perception problem; the braking is not. In the only FIR-level Indian crash dataset published, trucks were the most common impacting vehicle at 30%. DGS001 supplies detection, classification, tracking and per-target TTC on a documented interface, with confidence and sensor-health state. Actuation, calibration, homologation and warranty stay with the Tier-1 — that division is what makes the sale possible, and abandoning it is what makes it impossible. Forward camera into DGS001: detect and classify car, truck, bus, two- and three-wheeler, pedestrian and animal from 25 km/h to max design speed, at every load state Track each target, estimate range-rate, compute per-target TTC and in-path probability Emit a ranked object list with per-object confidence and a degradation state on the interface the Tier-1 specifies Tier-1 arbitrates the warning cascade and owns the braking decision and its safety case No published ISO 26262 pathway. Until an assessor is engaged the integrator is comparing a certified 5m-unit incumbent with an uncertified newcomer, and no perception result closes that gap. A braking Tier-1 accepts the interface, diagnostics, safety assumptions and validation plan in a written technical exchange, with a recorded go/no-go.

units.title: The claim still available is the false alarm, not the detection
units.body: Four rivals already claim India tuning — Aptiv publishes Indian object classes, STRADVISION cites dense mixed traffic, Netrasemi is Indian silicon, Starkenn markets Made-in-India. India-native is no longer a differentiator. What no competitor has published is a measured nuisance rate, and AIS-162 tests for exactly that: pass between two stationary vehicles at 50 km/h over 60 m, in silence. Instrument DGS001 for the denominator rather than the headline. Publish a scenario-stratified false-positive rate per 1,000 km against a named baseline on the same SoC class, the same functions and the same test set. This is the one lever in the STRADVISION contest whose result is genuinely open. Define the India nuisance set: overtaking two-wheelers, cut-in three-wheelers, cattle, roadside encroachment, unlit stationary trucks, wrong-way traffic, kerbside vending Log every trigger and every non-trigger with scenario tags across the three paid pilots, with telemetry rights secured in the contract Score false positives per 1,000 km and true-positive recall stratified by scenario, lighting and monsoon Publish at equal scope; withhold any comparison that silently changes what is being compared A nuisance rate without a denominator is marketing. If the scenario mix, kilometres and baseline are not fixed in advance, the result cannot be defended in a Tier-1 review and will be discounted to zero. One published equal-scope benchmark: named baseline, same SoC class, same function set, same test set, with scenario-stratified denominators and an independent test agency's protocol.

units.title: Two-thirds of India's road deaths are the road users these two standards were written for
units.body: Two-wheeler riders were 46.2% of India's 1,77,175 road deaths in 2024 and pedestrians 20.6% — together 1.28 lakh people. AIS-186 demands an information signal 15 m before the expected collision point with a cyclist on the passenger side, and forbids manual deactivation. AIS-187 demands detection of VRUs crossing at 3–5 km/h inside a 3.7 m forward plane. One India-trained perception core, two output contracts: near-field side and near-field front. Same silicon and same corpus, different detection geometry and signal timing. These are the two functions where India's VRU mix is the requirement itself rather than an edge case bolted onto a Western baseline. Side and front near-field cameras into DGS001; classify pedestrian, adult cyclist and child cyclist BSIS: project turn geometry including the counter-turn, raise the information signal at least 15 m before the collision point and hold it through the manoeuvre MOIS: detect VRUs crossing at 3–5 km/h and cyclists parallel at 0–10 km/h inside the 3.7 m plane; hold the signal through a standstill until 15 m past the stopping point Pass the false-information tests, including the BSIS traffic-sign case The BSIS information signal cannot be switched off, so a high nuisance rate here is not merely annoying — it is permanently in the driver's peripheral vision. UC-02's denominator work is a prerequisite, not a parallel track. A characterised near-field detection result against the AIS-186 and AIS-187 test geometries, with the false-information cases run, from an independent agency rather than a bench demonstration.

units.title: The only mandated function whose approval evidence is a human-subject study, not a track run
units.body: AIS-184 binds M2/M3/N2/N3 above 60 km/h design speed. Approval is not a track test: the manufacturer must run at least ten participants, none from the development team, in both day and night, generating ten or more true-positive or false-negative events, and report per-participant sensitivity with its standard deviation. Over-speeding drove 70.3% of India's 2024 road deaths; fatigue on long-haul highway runs is its companion. An in-cab drowsiness pipeline on the same DGS001 core, delivered together with the validation study that makes it approvable. The differentiator here is not the model. It is being the supplier who hands the integrator a completed AIS-184 documentation package instead of a demonstration. In-cab infrared camera into DGS001: eyelid closure, gaze, head pose and PERCLOS-class metrics, working at night Fuse with vehicle signals — reduced steering micro-corrections paired with larger, faster corrections, and lateral lane-position variability Warn above KSS level 8, optionally from level 7; escalate visual then acoustic per the HMI specification Run the ten-participant day-and-night study and deliver metrics, thresholds, activation speed, weather limits and the statistical analysis Intra-city buses, school buses and double-deckers are outside AIS-184 scope unless the manufacturer opts in. Sizing this use case against all M2/M3 volume overstates it, and an urban-bus fleet is the wrong first pilot. A completed ten-participant day-and-night validation study with per-participant sensitivity and standard deviation, plus the full documentation package a testing agency can assess.

units.title: The function India's road surface makes hardest and the mandate makes unavoidable
units.body: 58.6% of India's 2024 road deaths were on national and state highways that are roughly 5% of the network, and 67.6% of accidents happened on straight roads — precisely where LDWS applies. Yet markings on those corridors are worn, inconsistent or absent, and Indian lane discipline is informal by design. A stack tuned on painted European lanes alerts continuously here, and a continuously alerting LDWS gets switched off. Lane estimation that does not depend on a painted line. Road edge, kerb, median, worn marking and vehicle-flow cues fused into a drivable-corridor estimate, with departure thresholds that move with traffic density and speed rather than sitting fixed. Forward camera into DGS001: segment lane marking, road edge, kerb and median, and estimate marking quality Estimate the drivable corridor and lateral position when no marking is visible Modulate the departure threshold by traffic density and speed; suppress during indicated manoeuvres Emit the departure event with confidence, plus an explicit temporarily-unavailable state when the corridor cannot be estimated Declaring the function unavailable too readily is the easy way to pass a nuisance target and the fast way to fail type approval. Availability rate must be reported next to the false-alert rate or neither number means anything. A measured corridor-estimation and departure-alert result on unmarked and degraded Indian highway sections, reporting availability rate alongside false-alert rate.

OEM design-in runs 18 to 30 months, so line-fit revenue cannot arrive first. Every rupee before H1 2028 must come from the FPGA module, and only one arena gates on eligibility rather than certification. Package DGS001 as a GeM-listed, Class-I local-content perception kit for state transport undertakings and PSU fleets. At 50% or more local content DeepGrid is a Class-I local supplier with a 20% margin of purchase preference — and where a nodal ministry certifies sufficient local capacity, only Class-I suppliers may bid at all. Compute and document local content at or above 50%, self-certified with the locations of value addition List on GeM with country of origin and local-content percentage, qualifying for the Make in India filter Bid into STU, PSU and municipal tenders that are reserved for, or preference-weighted toward, Class-I suppliers Instrument every delivered unit and secure telemetry rights in the supply contract — these units are the evidence engine for UC-02 Starkenn already draws about 30% of revenue from government tenders and can underbid on empanelment, where eligibility rather than certification decides. Class-I status is winnable but slowly, and a nodal ministry may prescribe local content above 50%. A GeM listing live with a documented local-content percentage at or above 50%, and one tender bid submitted under Class-I preference with telemetry rights in the draft contract.

units.title: The demand is legislated, not forecast
units.body: Why now The demand is legislated, not forecast India is putting ADAS into law for commercial vehicles function by function, each with its own standard and its own date. Read at the standards level, the version that survives diligence, the schedule is this: AEBS (AIS-162, CMVR 96(12)) binds new models 1 Jan 2027 and all models 1 Oct 2027; drowsiness, blind-spot, moving-off and lane-departure warning (AIS-184/186/187/188, CMVR 125Q and 98(6)) bind new models 1 Oct 2027 and all models 1 Jan 2028. 0M units. Four functions arriving on one clock is the commercial fact that matters. Every CV maker must source drowsiness, blind-spot, moving-off and lane-departure together, so a supplier that carries more than one of the four from a single perception core is materially easier to nominate than four separate suppliers. That, rather than any single function, is the design-in argument.

units.title: The silicon
units.body: Here is the part itself. Thirty-two thousand seven hundred and sixty-eight multiply-accumulate units at six hundred megahertz, a hundred and two gigabytes a second of memory bandwidth, hardware softmax, and lockstep cores for the automotive safety path. The number that matters most: it fuses eleven sensor channels in eight point six milliseconds of a thirty-three millisecond frame. Seventy-four percent of the frame is left unused, and that headroom is why one die becomes fifteen products.

units.body: This is the first product where the silicon closes the loop instead of advising. Cameras and depth sensing read the aisle, the load and the people in it. What the silicon does here
Indoor autonomy is where the silicon runs closed-loop rather than advisory. A 24 m LiDAR at 5 Hz and a 57° camera fuse into one bird’s-eye occupancy view, and the planner drives to it at up to 1.5 m/s inside a ring-fenced safety zone — the vehicle steers, not the driver.

units.body: The demand is legislated, not forecast. Driver-drowsiness, blind-spot and lane-departure obligations land on new and existing commercial vehicles on fixed dates. About a million trucks a year fall in scope. For a fleet operator the question is not whether to buy — it is whose chip is inside when they do.

units.title: The move (spoken, slide 004)
units.body: The whole plan is downstream of one 28 nanometre part, and the programme is deliberately gated. Prove the compute and radar blocks first. Then the full die. Then backend sign-off. The production mask — the largest single commitment — is only paid for once working silicon exists.

units.title: The silicon (spoken, slide 005)
units.body: Here is the part itself. Thirty-two thousand seven hundred and sixty-eight multiply-accumulate units at six hundred megahertz, a hundred and two gigabytes a second of memory bandwidth, hardware softmax, and lockstep cores for the automotive safety path. The number that matters most: it fuses eleven sensor channels in eight point six milliseconds of a thirty-three millisecond frame. Seventy-four percent of the frame is left unused, and that headroom is why one die becomes fifteen products.

units.title: The portfolio (spoken, slide 006)
units.body: All fifteen, ranked by revenue in the final year. Prices are held flat across six years, so growth comes from volume, not from price. Note how far the list ranges — fifty thousand rupees for a mirror unit, eighteen thousand for a bare die, several lakh for a truck kit. Same silicon, priced independently by the market it sells into.

units.title: Part one — Road autonomy (spoken, slide 007)
units.body: Road autonomy is two-thirds of the plan: seven hundred and sixty-two crore, three SKUs. This is where the mandate acts, and where the concentration risk sits. Take these three carefully.

units.title: AD0 · What it is (spoken, slide 008)
units.body: A replacement rear-view mirror with a display built in, four small body cameras and a loom. Fifty thousand rupees, fitted in an afternoon. It is the least sophisticated thing we make and it ships first, on current-generation hardware.

units.title: AD0 · How it works (spoken, slide 009)
units.body: Four cameras cover the quarters a driver cannot see. The chip stitches them into a single surround view and watches the danger zone for anything entering it. The driver gets a stitched image and a directional chime. No braking, no steering — it informs, and that is the whole product.

units.title: AD0 · Who buys it (spoken, slide 010)
units.body: No mandate applies here, which is exactly the point: it already sells on its own merits. Owners and small fleets buy it as an accessory, through fitment shops and accessory catalogues, for visibility and parking. Demand does not wait for a compliance date.

units.title: AD1 · What it is (spoken, slide 012)
units.body: A self-driving retrofit kit for vehicles that never leave a building: a sensor head, a compute box, and a drive-by-wire interface. One lakh rupees. Fitted to forklifts and tugs a site already owns.

units.title: AD1 · How it works (spoken, slide 013)
units.body: This is the first product where the silicon closes the loop instead of advising. Cameras and depth sensing read the aisle, the load and the people in it. The chip localises against a site map it holds onboard. A planner picks a path and a speed. Then drive-by-wire actually steers, accelerates and brakes. The vehicle drives; the driver is not there.

units.body: Warehouse and industrial operators, direct or through material-handling integrators. Inside a private site no homologation applies, so this is a commercial decision, not a regulatory one — which is why level-four behaviour ships here years before it is legal on a public road.

units.title: AD1 · How it fits (spoken, slide 015)
units.body: Forty-two crore, under four percent of revenue. Small in the model and large in the argument: it is the technical proof point for the road roadmap, running the same silicon in a place where it is allowed to make the decision.

units.body: We built a drawable warehouse floor for this. You author the route, place workers, peer vehicles, trolleys and spills as obstacles, and run it. The alert policy is configurable — honk, voice, both, silent — because that is a site decision, not ours. And recovery is explicit: it reroutes after a set stuck-time.

units.body: Here it is, actually running. Inbound put-away, then a pick run, then the peak-hour floor. Watch the safety ring travelling with the truck and gating its speed, and watch the sensor-fusion panel top right build the bird's-eye view. units.title: AD2 · What it is (spoken, slide 018)
units.body: The Smart Truck kit — forward camera, radar, compute box, driver display and the harness that talks to the vehicle. Two and a half lakh rupees. This is the biggest single line in the plan and the one the mandate is written for.

units.title: AD2 · How it works (spoken, slide 019)
units.body: Camera and radar watch the forward path and the blind quarters. The chip fuses both into one object list carrying range and closing speed. Collision, lane and blind-spot logic decide whether to warn. The driver is warned, and where the vehicle supports it, the brake interface is signalled. Radar matters here because closing speed is what a braking decision actually turns on.

units.title: AD2 · Who buys it (spoken, slide 020)
units.body: Fleet operators and truck manufacturers, and the decision is compliance-led rather than discretionary. Retrofit through installers now; factory-fit is the longer, larger route. The buying question is which supplier, on what date.

units.title: AD2 · How it fits (spoken, slide 021)

units.title: AD2 · Proven in a simulator (spoken, slide 022)
units.body: Three road profiles — market street, single-carriageway highway, and a deliberate stress test — run against the same perception stack. The vehicle model is real: five hundred and fifty kilograms, two point one metre wheelbase, tyre friction of nought point seven five. Steering angle and lateral acceleration are solved, not scripted.

units.body: Watch the planner view in the centre. It redraws from the fused object list, not from an animation path. On the right, the perception rail names what it sees and how far away it is — a motorbike at twenty-six metres, an auto-rickshaw at thirty-eight. Three road profiles, one stack, nothing reloaded between them.

units.title: Sensor to compute · Eleven inputs (spoken, slide 024)
units.body: Before the silicon section, look at what the truck kit actually hands the compute. Seven colour cameras — road left and right, side left and right, a dashcam, a driver-monitoring camera and a rear camera. Two thermal cameras, one in each mirror tower. Radar at both ends for range and relative motion. Eleven configured inputs arriving at one in-cab processor, and one perception platform leaving it. For the fleet operator the installation is a single application, not eleven integrations.

units.title: Sensor to compute · The compute box, running (spoken, slide 025)
units.body: And here it is moving. Watch the eleven channels converge on the die, and one AD2 stream leave it. The bar underneath is the frame budget: eight point six milliseconds against thirty-three point three. Treat that as an architecture illustration — the next two slides set out exactly what would have to be measured before it becomes a claim.

units.title: Sensor to compute · Each sensor's job (spoken, slide 026)
units.body: The eleven are not redundancy. Each tower carries a road camera, a hundred-and-twenty-degree side camera and a thermal camera, so the same quarter is seen three ways in different physics. Radar covers both ends, where cameras are weakest in rain and glare. Inside the cab the dashcam records and the driver-monitoring camera watches the driver — different tasks on different data. What stays open is calibration, occlusion, mounting, and the final sensor list.

units.title: AD2 · G · Sensor coverage (spoken, slide 027)
units.body: Before we leave the truck kit, look at the sensor layout it actually ships. Two towers retrofit above the existing mirrors, each with a thermal camera, a road camera and a hundred-and-twenty-degree side camera. Two cameras in the cab. Four-D radar front and rear. Watch the coverage cones sweep and overlap — the claim the layout makes is that no quarter of a heavy truck goes unobserved.

units.title: Sensor to compute · Define the measurement (spoken, slide 028)
units.body: This is the discipline that number still needs. Thirty-three point three milliseconds is about thirty frames a second. Eight point six of them is the processing claim, which leaves roughly twenty-four point seven — but that is budget subtraction, not measured headroom. Three things have to be fixed before it is a claim: which acquisition, inference and fusion stages sit inside the measurement, the precision and sustained rate, and the worst case rather than the average.
questions: What methodological flaws exist in the reported 8.6 millisecond processing claim?
What measurements are required to substantiate the system's speed and latency claims?

units.title: Sensor to compute · Prove it in stages (spoken, slide 029)
units.body: The proving is staged, because the stages answer different questions. An FPGA demonstration exercises the software, the interfaces and prototype compute. ASIC verification checks scaled compute, memory, clock, power and area together — none of which an FPGA can tell you. Vehicle qualification tests thermal behaviour, the safety path and real operating conditions. Confidence should track the evidence at each stage rather than run ahead of it.
questions: What specific risks do FPGAs fail to uncover before ASIC tapeout?

units.title: Sensor to compute · The ladder, running (spoken, slide 030)
units.body: That staging already has a history. Nine steps, and five of them are silicon: each rung added one block and then measured the frame rate that followed. Watch the bars fill as it climbs. SoC2 is what this raise funds — thirty-two thousand seven hundred and sixty-eight multiply-accumulates at six hundred megahertz, tapeout in the fourth quarter of twenty twenty-six. The frame rates are management figures, not third-party benchmarks.

units.title: Part two — Silicon and compute (spoken, slide 031)
units.body: Now the half of the business that sells the chip instead of the vehicle. A hundred and ninety-four crore across five SKUs, and the highest margins in the plan — because none of these need an installation crew.

units.title: Chipset OEM · What it is (spoken, slide 032)
units.body: The bare die, in tray or reel, for a customer to place on their own board. Eighteen thousand rupees. No enclosure, no cables, no fitting — we ship silicon and a datasheet, and the customer does the rest.

units.title: Chipset OEM · How it works (spoken, slide 033)
units.body: The customer's own sensors feed their own board. Our die does the perception compute inside their design. Their software decides what to do with the result, and their product ships with our silicon inside it. We supply one stage of someone else's chain.
questions: Who is responsible for the application software when customers buy our bare die?

units.title: Chipset OEM · Who buys it (spoken, slide 034)
units.body: Manufacturers who want Indian-designed silicon and domestic supply rather than an imported part, and who have the engineering to integrate it. Procurement policy is often as decisive as specification here.
questions: What motivates OEMs to choose our domestic silicon over established imported alternatives?

units.title: Chipset OEM · How it fits (spoken, slide 035)
units.body: Fifty-four crore at ninety-four percent gross margin — the highest in the portfolio. Every rupee here arrives without installation capacity, warranty logistics or a fitment channel behind it.

Why does this product line avoid traditional warranty logistics and installation overhead?

units.title: Compute and data · Compute waits (spoken, slide 036)
units.body: Now the half of the business that sells the chip itself, and the problem that shapes it. Eight processing cores behind one dispatch point: the cores are not the constraint, the queue is. Give each core its own address generation and its own transfers and they proceed independently — though parallel requests still compete for finite service capacity. The four-hundred-and-seventy to eighty-five millisecond figure is a proposal awaiting testbench evidence, and the deck says so on the slide.
questions: Are those latency reduction figures backed by benchmark data, or are they unproven proposals?
What is the primary bottleneck preventing processing cores from reaching maximum throughput?
How does decoupling the processing cores impact parallel memory requests?

units.title: Compute and data · Shared engine, running (spoken, slide 037)
units.body: Watch the two run side by side. On the left, one data engine and seven cores waiting their turn. On the right, the same silicon with an engine per core. The utilisation columns are the whole point — short and flat on the left, filled and held on the right. Illustrative dispatch, not a measured application speedup.
questions: Is the reported utilization improvement based on actual hardware measurements or just illustrative simulations?
What difference does adding an independent data engine per core make to overall efficiency?

units.title: Compute and data · Inside one local DMA (spoken, slide 038)
units.body: What actually sits inside one of those local engines. A descriptor names the transfer parameters and the data layout. A three-level address engine walks the tensor without asking a central dispatcher for every step. A read FIFO absorbs the gap between when memory serves and when compute consumes. The cost is roughly six hundred lookup tables each — about four thousand eight hundred for eight — plus arbitration logic and the firmware to drive it.
questions: What is the silicon footprint cost in lookup tables for implementing these local engines?
How do local DMAs handle tensor traversal without bogging down the central dispatcher?
What components make up the internal architecture of a local DMA engine?

units.title: Compute and data · Placement is a choice (spoken, slide 039)
units.body: Step back from our own design and the useful comparison is not who has a DMA. It is who schedules the movement, where the data sits, and what has to cross the chip. A shared engine schedules for several cores. Local controllers issue requests nearer the compute they serve, so more data stays local — and then software carries the burden of mapping and coordinating it. The outcome is decided by workload results, compiler mapping and implementation IP, not by the data mover alone.
questions: How does your data movement strategy differ from standard DMA architectures?
Does your hardware design shift the complexity burden onto the software and compiler?
What actually determines real-world workload performance beyond just the data mover?
Is your local controller approach more efficient than a shared engine for data locality?

units.title: Compute and data · The memory spectrum (spoken, slide 040)
units.body: Six chips, six answers to that question. From our own shared-DMA arrangement today, through Mobileye's VLIW cores on a shared level-two cache and NVIDIA's brute-force parallelism, out to Tesla's Dojo, where every core holds private SRAM and the die carries no DRAM at all. Per-core DMA against a shared level-two cache sits in the middle, and that middle is where most of the industry already is. Vendor figures here come from public sources.
questions: How does your memory architecture compare to NVIDIA's parallelism or Tesla's Dojo?
Where does your chip sit on the spectrum between shared cache and private SRAM?
Are you just following the industry average for memory controller placement?
Why does your design lack the private SRAM benefits seen in Dojo?

units.title: Compute and data · Eight layers (spoken, slide 041)
units.body: This is where the eight-times figure comes from, stated carefully. Sixty-four multiply-accumulate positions process the reduction depth across iterations. Five hundred and twelve positions express that depth in hardware instead. Compare the same K-equals-eight tile at the same precision and the arithmetic ratio is eight. It is an idealised comparison — pipeline fill, tensor shapes, data reuse and memory delivery all still apply.
questions: What is the technical justification for your 8x performance claim?
Is the 8x arithmetic ratio based on idealized conditions rather than real-world usage?
How do you account for pipeline stalls and memory delivery in your performance figures?
How does your hardware reduction depth compare to standard MAC positions?

units.title: Chipset · E · The compute (spoken, slide 042)
units.body: And this is what the customer is actually buying, running. On the left, the flat eight-by-eight matrix as it works on the FPGA today: sixty-four multiply-accumulates a cycle, iterating the reduction in software. On the right, the cube on twenty-eight nanometre silicon, where that reduction becomes hardware depth and all eight layers fire at once. Watch the tile counters diverge — that gap is the eight-times figure, shown rather than claimed.
questions: What is the performance delta between your current FPGA prototype and the final 28nm silicon?
How much of your speedup is simply moving software iterations into hardware logic?
Can you prove the 8x throughput increase without relying on theoretical tile counters?
What is the actual compute density of your 28nm cube design?

units.title: Compute and data · A stronger data path (spoken, slide 043)
units.body: Which is what the section has been building to. More arithmetic increases the demand for data; it does not satisfy it. Independent controllers remove one serialisation point, but memory mapping and arbitration still decide which requests complete. Compute geometry, data movement and physical implementation are one design problem, not three. Measure useful work — peak TOPS on its own says nothing about utilisation.
questions: Are your peak TOPS figures a misleading metric for actual hardware utilization?
How do you prevent data starvation as you scale up arithmetic units?
Does your architecture solve the memory arbitration bottleneck or just move it?
Why should we trust your data path if utilization isn't being measured directly?

units.title: Compute and data · Follow one tile (spoken, slide 044)
units.body: Follow a single tile end to end. External memory feeds the shared on-chip storage. Eight banks serve requests according to mapping and arbitration. Fifty-six local movers each supply their own compute cube. The figure quoted here — fifty-six times five hundred and twelve multiply-accumulates, at six hundred megahertz, times two operations — is an arithmetic peak, and the slide is explicit that it is not a benchmark.
questions: What is the theoretical peak arithmetic throughput of a single tile?
How does the shared on-chip storage distribute data to the 56 local movers?
Is your 600MHz clock speed competitive for this type of compute cube?
Are these figures actual benchmarks or just marketing math?

units.title: Compute and data · A hot bank (spoken, slide 045)
units.body: And here is the failure mode, with the workload held constant. Spread evenly, fifty-six requests give seven per bank. Collide them all onto bank zero and seven banks sit idle while the array stalls. Spread the addresses again and the capacity returns. What decides which of those you get is tensor layout, address hashing, arbitration and compiler scheduling — and the request counts here are a controlled illustration, not measured utilisation.
questions: How does the system handle memory bank collisions and array stalls?
What is the worst-case performance hit when tensor layouts cause bank contention?
Is your compiler smart enough to prevent idle banks during complex workloads?
Are your utilization figures based on real-world software or controlled simulations?

units.title: Compute and data · Freeze, then measure (spoken, slide 046)
units.body: So the honest close to this section. A production advantage is demonstrated by the whole platform, never by a multiplier count. Freeze the core count, the precision, the clock and the bandwidth. Then measure sustained throughput and worst-case latency on representative tensors, with power, area, safety architecture and silicon status recorded beside them. Arithmetic peaks at six hundred megahertz are not measured application throughput, and this deck does not offer them as such.
questions: What is the sustained throughput and worst-case latency on representative tensors?
Are you hiding poor application performance behind theoretical 600MHz peaks?
How does the safety architecture and silicon area impact your total performance envelope?
Why hasn't the company provided measured application throughput yet?

units.title: A100 four-channel · What it is (spoken, slide 055)

units.body: Four channels demands the memory bandwidth the compute geometry was designed around. Each compute cube runs its own local memory access against a banked cache, which is what keeps utilisation high instead of starving on a single shared path. units.body: Customers building full surround perception who want the compute inside their own architecture rather than in a box we supply — robotics platforms, industrial vehicles, and anyone who already has a host machine and needs to add sight to it.

units.body: Thirty-six crore, the largest of the three compute boxes. Together the A100 family is ninety crore of revenue that needs no vehicle, no installer and no homologation.

units.body: Not hardware at all. A licence to the trained perception models and the toolchain, so a customer can run our software on their own platform. Priced per deployment, with nothing shipped in a box.

units.title: T100 licence · How it works (spoken, slide 060)
units.body: The models are the accumulated result of running these sensors on Indian roads. A customer licences that, integrates it, and ships. There is no board, no bill of materials, and nothing to manufacture.
questions: What is actually being sold with the T100 licence if there is no bill of materials?
How do Indian road datasets power the T100 software models?
Is there any hardware manufacturing involved in the T100 licence model?

units.title: T100 licence · Who buys it (spoken, slide 061)
units.body: Teams that want perception tuned for Indian road conditions — the traffic mix, the lane discipline, the light — without spending three years collecting the data to train it themselves. The dataset is the product here, not the code.
questions: Why would a customer buy the T100 licence instead of collecting their own training data?
What specific driving conditions are the T100 perception models tuned for?
Is the dataset considered the primary product value for T100 buyers?

units.title: T100 licence · How it fits (spoken, slide 062)
units.body: Fifty crore at ninety-four percent margin, and it starts later than everything else — in the 2029 financial year — because a licence needs a track record before anyone buys one. It is the only line in the plan with no bill of materials whatsoever.
questions: What is the projected gross margin for the T100 licence?
Why does T100 revenue only start in the 2029 financial year?
Why does this line item have zero bill of materials and how defensible is that high margin really?

units.title: Part three — Fleet and mobility (spoken, slide 063)
units.body: Two SKUs, eighty-nine crore, and the highest revenue per unit anywhere in the portfolio. Here we stop selling a product and start selling the work the product does.
questions: What is the total revenue of the fleet and mobility SKUs?
Why is the revenue per unit the highest in the entire portfolio for this segment?
How does the business model shift from selling products to selling outcomes in fleet and mobility?

units.title: TaaS · What it is (spoken, slide 064)
units.body: Not a sale. A vehicle we own and operate under contract, where the customer pays for the transport rather than the truck. The revenue per unit is the largest in the plan because we are booking the whole job.
questions: How does the Transport-as-a-Service model work commercially?
Why is the TaaS revenue per unit the largest in the financial plan?
Are customers paying for the underlying truck or just the transport service under TaaS?

units.title: TaaS · How it works (spoken, slide 065)
units.body: The vehicle runs the same autonomy stack as the kit we sell. Fleet logic schedules it, routes it, and hands off to a remote operator when the situation exceeds what the vehicle should decide alone. The difference from AD2 is commercial, not technical.
questions: How does TaaS differ technically from the AD2 autonomy stack?
What role do remote operators play when autonomous fleet vehicles encounter complex situations?
How do fleet logic and remote intervention handle edge cases in TaaS operations?

units.title: TaaS · Who buys it (spoken, slide 066)
units.body: Operators comparing cost per tonne-kilometre against a driven alternative — and increasingly comparing against driver availability rather than driver cost, because on many routes the constraint is finding a driver at all.
questions: What drives fleet operators to adopt TaaS instead of traditional trucks?
Is driver scarcity a bigger factor than driver wages in the shift to TaaS?
How do customers evaluate the economics of TaaS versus human-driven transport?

units.title: TaaS · How it fits (spoken, slide 067)
units.body: Sixty-six crore. It is the line that shows what the technology is worth when we capture the operating margin instead of the hardware margin. It also carries operational risk the product lines do not: we own the asset and the uptime.
questions: What is the revenue or financial value attributed to the TaaS segment?
Why does capturing operating margin instead of hardware margin introduce new risks?
Are we taking on asset ownership and uptime liabilities by moving into TaaS?

units.title: Seaport AGV · What it is (spoken, slide 068)
units.body: An autonomous container-yard vehicle working inside a port perimeter. A controlled site, but not an easy one: heavy equipment overhead, tight lanes between stacks, and real consequences for a positioning error.
questions: What is the Seaport AGV product and where is it deployed?
How difficult is the operating environment for port automation vehicles?
What are the main physical hazards container-yard vehicles face on site?

units.title: Seaport AGV · How it works (spoken, slide 069)
units.body: Under a quay crane, satellite positioning degrades exactly where precision matters most. Sensor fusion on our silicon holds seven centimetres in the open and twenty-two under the crane, where satellite alone falls away. That positioning is what makes crane-synchronised dispatch possible at all.
questions: How does the AGV maintain positioning accuracy when satellite signals drop under quay cranes?
What level of positioning precision does the sensor fusion achieve in the open versus under the crane?
Why is high-precision positioning critical for crane-synchronised dispatch?

units.title: Seaport AGV · Who buys it (spoken, slide 070)
units.body: Terminal operators, measured on throughput and labour cost inside a geofenced site. No public-road homologation applies, so adoption is limited by operational confidence rather than regulation.
questions: Who is the target customer for the Seaport AGV and what metrics do they care about?
Does port AGV deployment require public-road homologation or regulatory approval?
What is the primary bottleneck slowing down seaport AGV adoption if regulation is not an issue?

units.title: Seaport AGV · How it fits (spoken, slide 071)
units.body: Twenty-two and a half crore. Read its market share differently from the others: the sized pool is total port automation including cranes and software, and we sell only the vehicle layer.
questions: What is the financial valuation or market size figure associated with the Seaport AGV?
How misleading is our market share calculation given that we only sell the vehicle layer of total port automation?
Does our addressable market figure include port software and cranes or just our hardware?

units.title: Seaport AGV · Proven in a simulator (spoken, slide 072)
units.body: A working twin of a container terminal, built to prove the three things the programme asks for: that positioning holds where satellite fails, that routing copes with congestion, and that scheduling collapses crane idle time. It runs in shadow mode first — advising the terminal before it is given control.
questions: What does the container terminal digital twin simulate to de-risk the programme?
How does shadow mode testing work before the system is given live control?
Can the simulator prove that routing handles congestion and eliminates crane idle time?

units.title: Seaport AGV · The simulator, running (spoken, slide 073)
units.body: Quay discharge, then the container canyon, then peak mixed traffic. Watch the two confidence bars diverge as the vehicle enters the canyon — satellite drops, fusion holds. The trial panel on the right carries the numbers: seven centimetres open, twenty-two under crane, nine percent error on arrival time.
questions: What do the confidence bars show when an AGV enters the container canyon?
What are the exact performance metrics displayed on the trial panel during simulation?
How much does positioning degrade under the crane compared to open areas?

units.title: Part four — Sensors and robotics (spoken, slide 074)
units.body: Five SKUs, eighty-three and a half crore. Two purposes: sensors that make the main products work in conditions where cameras fail, and robotics platforms that put the same silicon into a second market cycle.
questions: How many SKUs are in the sensors and robotics division and what is their financial contribution?
What are the dual purposes of the sensors and robotics portfolio?
Are these robotics platforms meant to monetize the same silicon through a secondary market cycle?

units.title: Thermal camera · What it is (spoken, slide 075)
units.body: A bolt-on long-wave infrared pod with its own lens and heater, feeding the compute box. Forty thousand rupees. It is an accessory to the systems above it, not a standalone product.
questions: What is the thermal camera accessory and how much does it cost?
Can this thermal infrared pod be sold as a standalone product or only as an add-on?
What hardware components are included in the thermal camera pod?

units.title: Thermal camera · How it works (spoken, slide 076)
units.body: It reads emitted heat rather than reflected light, so a person or an animal separates from the background in the dark, through glare, dust and smoke. The chip runs detection on the thermal image alongside the visible one. This is the channel that keeps working when the others stop.
questions: How does the thermal sensor perform in bad weather or total darkness?
Why does the thermal camera work when other vision systems fail?
Does the thermal channel operate independently from the visible camera?
Can thermal imaging really cut through dust, smoke, and glare?

units.title: Thermal camera · Who buys it (spoken, slide 077)
units.body: Fleets running at night and through the monsoon, where camera-only detection degrades sharply. It is sold as an upgrade to a system already fitted, which makes it a second sale into an existing customer rather than a new acquisition.
questions: Who actually buys the thermal camera add-on?
Is the thermal unit sold as a standalone product or an upsell?
Which fleet segments are the primary target for thermal imaging upgrades?
How hard is it to cross-sell the thermal module to existing clients?

units.title: Thermal camera · How it fits (spoken, slide 078)
units.body: Sixteen crore at fifty percent gross margin — half the group average, because a sensor carries real component cost. Its job is to raise the capability of the products around it, not to carry the plan.
questions: What is the revenue contribution and margin profile of the thermal camera?
Why is the gross margin on thermal sensors so much lower than the company average?
Is thermal imaging just a feature enhancer rather than a core revenue driver?
What is the financial sizing for the thermal camera product line?

units.title: 4D radar · What it is (spoken, slide 079)
units.body: A sealed radar pod, mounted forward or on a corner, feeding the same compute box. Twenty-five thousand rupees, and weatherproof by design because it has to work in the conditions that defeat everything else.
questions: What is the unit price and hardware specification of the 4D radar pod?
How is the 4D radar unit mounted and integrated into the vehicle?
Can the radar hardware withstand harsh environmental conditions?
Why is a sealed radar pod necessary for this architecture?

units.title: 4D radar · How it works (spoken, slide 080)
units.body: It illuminates the scene and reads the returns, and the radar block on the die turns those returns into range, velocity and angle. Tracks are held across frames, including through rain and dust. Radar supplies closing speed — the one quantity a camera estimates and a radar measures.
questions: How does 4D radar measure target velocity compared to standard cameras?
Can radar reliably track objects through heavy rain and dust?
Why is radar better at calculating closing speed than a vision-only setup?
How does the processor handle radar returns across multiple frames?

units.title: 4D radar · Who buys it (spoken, slide 081)
units.body: Operations where weather and dust defeat cameras — and any application where a braking decision has to be defensible afterwards, because a measured closing speed stands up where an estimated one does not.
questions: Why would a fleet choose radar over cameras for critical braking decisions?
How does measured closing speed help with liability or accident investigation?
Which operational environments necessitate 4D radar deployment?
Is radar only being bought because cameras fail in bad weather?

units.title: 4D radar · How it fits (spoken, slide 082)
units.body: Seven and a half crore — the smallest line in the plan. It is here because the flagship product needs it, not because it is a business on its own.
questions: What is the revenue contribution of the 4D radar product line?
Is 4D radar actually a viable standalone business or just a checkbox feature?
Why is the radar budget so small compared to the rest of the portfolio?
If radar isn't a major revenue driver, why fund it at all?

units.title: H100 wearable · What it is (spoken, slide 083)
units.body: A wrist-worn band with on-body sensors and a radio link to the vehicle. Fifteen hundred rupees. It is driver monitoring without a camera pointed at the driver's face — the same obligation, answered a different way.
questions: What is the H100 wearable and how much does it cost?
How does the H100 replace in-cab driver monitoring cameras?
What is the retail price point for the driver wristband?
Why use a wrist-worn band instead of a standard cabin-facing camera?

units.title: H100 wearable · How it works (spoken, slide 084)
units.body: The band reads pulse and movement continuously, the vehicle correlates that with how the vehicle is being driven, and fatigue is flagged before it becomes a lane departure. It measures the driver directly rather than inferring from the road.
questions: How does the H100 wearable detect driver fatigue before an incident occurs?
What specific metrics does the wrist band continuously track?
How does the system correlate driver biometrics with vehicle behavior?
Is direct physiological measurement more reliable than road-based inference?

units.title: H100 wearable · Who buys it (spoken, slide 085)
units.body: Fleets meeting driver-drowsiness obligations that want a lower-intrusion option than an in-cab camera. Driver acceptance is a genuine adoption factor, and a wristband clears it more easily.
questions: Why do fleets prefer a wearable band over an in-cab monitoring camera?
Do drivers actually accept wearing biometric bands on shift?
How does the H100 help fleets comply with drowsiness regulations without causing pushback?
Is driver privacy resistance actually hurting camera-based monitoring adoption?

units.title: H100 wearable · How it fits (spoken, slide 086)
units.body: Ten crore at fifty percent margin. A hedge on how the drowsiness requirement is satisfied in practice, on a portfolio that otherwise answers it with a camera.
questions: What is the revenue and margin profile of the H100 wearable?
How does the H100 hedge against risks in the drowsiness monitoring requirements?
Why rely on a wearable for drowsiness when the rest of the portfolio uses a camera?
What is the financial contribution of the H100 wearable to the portfolio?

units.title: D-HUMR · What it is (spoken, slide 087)
units.body: An unmanned ground vehicle for defence logistics and reconnaissance. It is the only line in the portfolio selling to a government customer, and the only one whose buying cycle is measured in years rather than quarters.
questions: What is D-HUMR and what are its primary use cases?
How does D-HUMR differ from the rest of the portfolio in terms of customers and sales cycles?
Is D-HUMR the only product selling to government entities?
Why are D-HUMR's sales cycles measured in years instead of quarters?

units.title: D-HUMR · How it works (spoken, slide 088)
units.body: The same fusion stack, pointed outward instead of forward. Radar, thermal and camera tracks along a perimeter are classified individually, then correlated — so a vehicle loitering on an access road and a person approaching the fence stop being two unrelated contacts.
questions: How does the sensor fusion stack work on the D-HUMR platform?
Can D-HUMR correlate multiple threat types like vehicles and pedestrians?
How does D-HUMR combine radar, thermal, and camera data?
What prevents D-HUMR from treating a loitering vehicle and a person near a fence as unrelated events?

units.title: D-HUMR · Who buys it (spoken, slide 089)
units.body: Defence procurement, for tasks where sending a vehicle is preferable to sending people. Qualification is long and the cycles are slow — but once a platform is in, it is very hard to displace.
questions: Who is the target buyer for D-HUMR?
How difficult is it to displace D-HUMR once it wins a defence contract?
What are the main friction points in defence procurement for this product?
Why do defence buyers choose unmanned vehicles over sending personnel?

units.title: D-HUMR · How it fits (spoken, slide 090)
units.body: Thirty crore at sixty-eight percent margin. Its real value is strategic: a sovereign customer, a separate procurement route, and a use case that does not depend on the automotive mandate at all.
questions: What are the projected revenue and margins for D-HUMR?
Why is D-HUMR strategically valuable beyond its financials?
Does D-HUMR rely on automotive mandates for its market demand?
How does having a sovereign customer benefit the portfolio?

units.title: D-HUMR · Proven in a simulator (spoken, slide 091)
units.body: A live perimeter console. It correlates a vehicle track with a human track into one threat, escalates it along a timed ladder from loiter to approach to breach risk, and hands the target to ground sensors, a patrol drone or a sea buoy. The feature that matters is the restraint: benign tracks are held and never escalated, because false-alarm rate is what gets a perimeter system switched off.
questions: How does the D-HUMR console handle false alarms to prevent operators from switching it off?
What is the escalation ladder process on the D-HUMR perimeter console?
How are benign tracks managed so they don't trigger false alarms?
Which external sensors can D-HUMR hand targets over to?

units.title: D-HUMR · The simulator, running (spoken, slide 092)
units.body: Coordinated intrusion, then perimeter patrol, then a maritime approach. Watch two separate tracks fuse into one threat, and watch the escalation ladder on the right fill in — the operator sees intent forming rather than an alarm at the breach. The console states its reasoning in words.
questions: How does the D-HUMR simulator demonstrate intent formation during an intrusion?
Can the simulator show multi-domain threats like perimeter patrols and maritime approaches?
Does the operator interface explain its reasoning in plain text?
How does the escalation ladder display on the console during a breach?

units.title: D100 drone · What it is (spoken, slide 093)
units.body: A flight-capable compute and perception kit sold to airframe builders. It is the smallest and lightest configuration of the same silicon, constrained by weight and power rather than by cost.
questions: What is the D100 drone kit and who is it sold to?
How is the D100 constrained in terms of weight, power, and cost?
Is the D100 a complete aircraft or just a compute and perception kit?
Why use the same silicon for the D100 when it has stricter weight and power limits?

units.title: D100 drone · How it works (spoken, slide 094)
units.body: Cameras and an inertial unit read the scene and the airframe's own motion. The chip holds position and detects obstacles onboard, so the aircraft is not dependent on a radio link to stay safe. The flight controller executes.
questions: How does the D100 maintain position and avoid obstacles without a radio link?
What sensors does the D100 use to read scene and airframe motion?
Does the D100 rely on ground communication for flight safety?
How does the flight controller interact with the D100 perception kit?

units.title: D100 drone · Who buys it (spoken, slide 095)
units.body: Airframe builders with onboard autonomy requirements — inspection, survey, and any mission flown where the radio link cannot be relied upon. They buy compute, not aircraft, and they build the rest themselves.
questions: Who purchases the D100 drone compute kit?
What specific missions require the D100's offline autonomy capabilities?
Are these customers buying complete drones or just underlying compute hardware?
Why do airframe builders need onboard autonomy that works without radio links?

units.title: D100 drone · How it fits (spoken, slide 096)
units.body: Twenty crore. Treat it as optionality rather than base case: the same die, in a market with a different cycle and different buyers, entered without designing new silicon to get there.
questions: How much does the D100 drone project cost?
Is the D100 drone factored into our base case or just treated as optionality?
Does the drone require designing new silicon from scratch?
What is the capital allocation for the D100 drone?

units.title: Part five — Portfolio economics (spoken, slide 097)
units.body: Fifteen products explained. Now what they do together — concentration, timing, where the autonomy actually runs, where the margin is, and how much of each market we are assuming we win.
questions: What are the key themes of the portfolio economics section?
How do the fifteen products interact regarding concentration and margins?
What market share assumptions are baked into the portfolio plan?

units.title: Concentration (spoken, slide 098)
units.body: Be clear about this: two SKUs carry sixty-four percent. The truck kit and the smart mirror are the same product family sold to overlapping buyers, so a certification delay or an installation bottleneck hits seven hundred and twenty crore at once — more than the other thirteen SKUs combined. That is the single largest risk in the plan.
questions: What is the single largest risk in the entire plan?
How much revenue is tied up in the truck kit and smart mirror product family?
What happens if a certification delay or installation bottleneck hits our top SKUs?
Aren't we dangerously overexposed to just two SKUs driving sixty-four percent of the business?

units.title: Sequencing (spoken, slide 099)
units.body: Six SKUs earn revenue in the 2027 financial year, nine more in 2028. The 2027 revenue is one point seven crore across six products, on current-generation hardware — deliberately small. The ramp switches on when production silicon reaches market, and the licence line starts later still. The shape of this plan is gated by the chip, which is what the round funds.
questions: What is the revenue timeline and SKU rollout schedule across 2027 and 2028?
How much revenue is expected in the 2027 financial year?
What hardware is initial 2027 revenue running on?
What is the main gating factor for the entire plan's revenue ramp?

units.title: Where autonomy runs (spoken, slide 100)
units.body: Eighty-six percent of revenue runs outdoors, where public-road rules and homologation apply. Six percent runs indoors, geofenced, where level four ships years earlier on identical silicon. Eight percent is pure compute with no vehicle exposure at all. Same chip, three very different regulatory positions.
questions: Where does the autonomy actually execute across our revenue base?
What percentage of revenue is exposed to public-road rules and homologation?
How much of the revenue comes from geofenced indoor applications?
What proportion of the portfolio is pure compute with no vehicle exposure?

units.title: Margin (spoken, slide 101)
units.body: Volume and margin sit in different places, and that is the useful thing on this slide. Systems are eighty-three percent of revenue, so group economics track systems. But the marginal rupee is worth most in semiconductors at ninety-four percent, and those lines need no installation capacity. Growth in the silicon SKUs improves group margin without adding operational load.
questions: Where do volume and margin sit in the product portfolio?
Which product lines have the highest marginal profitability?
How do semiconductor sales impact group margins without adding operational load?
What percentage of revenue comes from systems versus silicon?

units.title: Headroom (spoken, slide 102)
units.body: No SKU in this plan assumes we win its market. Every line sits under two percent of its own sized demand pool, and most pools are global while our addressable market is the India slice — so the real share is higher than shown. Read the port line differently: that pool is total port automation, and we sell only the vehicle layer.
questions: What market share do we need to capture to hit our forecast numbers?
Are these projections based on winning dominant market share?
How are the addressable market pools sized relative to our sales assumptions?
Does the port automation line represent the entire port market or just a specific layer?

units.title: Far horizon · SoC4-A (spoken, slide 103)
units.body: One more part, and deliberately not the one this raise funds. SoC4-A is the far horizon: one thousand and twenty-four tiles on a four-nanometre process, four petaflops at FP4, assembled from published, silicon-proven blocks from the open PULP platform. It is optionality that sits outside this plan. SoC2 is the business; this is the option the business buys you.
questions: What is the SoC4-A chip and is it funded by this financing round?
What are the technical specifications of the SoC4-A architecture?
How does SoC2 relate to the far horizon SoC4-A optionality?
Is the SoC4-A development just an expensive distraction from the core business plan?

units.title: The ask (spoken, slide 104)
units.body: Fifteen products, one tapeout. The demand is legislated, the margin sits in silicon that needs no installation capacity, and no line in the plan requires us to win its market. Release the capital against silicon, certification and paying customers — not against the forecast. The portfolio is not fifteen bets. It is one bet, fifteen times over.
questions: What is the core investment thesis of this fundraising round?
What should investors actually be releasing capital against?
How many bets are we really making with these fifteen products?
Isn't a fifteen-product portfolio too diversified for a single tapeout?

units.title: Cover (spoken, slide 01)
units.body: Fifteen products. One chip. This is the long version — every SKU in the plan, what it physically is, how it runs on shared silicon, who pays for it, and what it contributes. Everything here is a management projection prepared for fundraising.
questions: How many products and chips are covered in this presentation?
What details are provided for each SKU in the plan?
Are these figures actual results or management projections for fundraising?
Who pays for these SKUs and what do they contribute financially?

units.title: How to read this deck (spoken, slide 02)
units.body: Each product gets the same four slides, in the same order: what it is, how it works, who buys it and why now, and how it fits. Four of them get two more, because a working simulator exists and you should watch it rather than take our word. Learn the pattern once and the next eighty slides navigate themselves.
questions: How is this investor deck structured?
Why do some product sections include a working simulator?

units.title: Why now (spoken, slide 03)
units.body: The demand is legislated, not forecast. Driver-drowsiness, blind-spot and lane-departure obligations land on new and existing commercial vehicles on fixed dates. About a million trucks a year fall in scope. For a fleet operator the question is not whether to buy — it is whose chip is inside when they do.
questions: What drives the demand for these commercial vehicle products?
How many trucks per year are impacted by these regulations?
Is fleet adoption driven by regulatory mandates or discretionary spending?
How certain is the addressable market size if compliance is legally required?

units.title: The move (spoken, slide 04)
units.body: The whole plan is downstream of one 28 nanometre part, and the programme is deliberately gated. Prove the compute and radar blocks first. Then the full die. Then backend sign-off. The production mask — the largest single commitment — is only paid for once working silicon exists.
questions: What is the underlying hardware foundation for this product roadmap?
How is the semiconductor development program risk-gated?
At what stage of development is the expensive production mask paid for?

units.title: The silicon (spoken, slide 05)
units.body: Here is the part itself. Thirty-two thousand seven hundred and sixty-eight multiply-accumulate units at six hundred megahertz, a hundred and two gigabytes a second of memory bandwidth, hardware softmax, and lockstep cores for the automotive safety path. The number that matters most: it fuses eleven sensor channels in eight point six milliseconds of a thirty-three millisecond frame. Seventy-four percent of the frame is left unused, and that headroom is why one die becomes fifteen products.
questions: What are the key technical specifications of the silicon chip?
How many sensor channels does the chip fuse and in what timeframe?
Why is there so much processing headroom left over in a frame?
How does a single die translate into fifteen different products?

units.title: The portfolio (spoken, slide 06)
units.body: All fifteen, ranked by revenue in the final year. Prices are held flat across six years, so growth comes from volume, not from price. Note how far the list ranges — fifty thousand rupees for a mirror unit, eighteen thousand for a bare die, several lakh for a truck kit. Same silicon, priced independently by the market it sells into.
questions: How are the fifteen SKUs priced and ranked?
Does revenue growth rely on pricing power or volume expansion?
What is the price range across the product portfolio?

units.title: Part one — Road autonomy (spoken, slide 07)
units.body: Road autonomy is two-thirds of the plan: seven hundred and sixty-two crore, three SKUs. This is where the mandate acts, and where the concentration risk sits. Take these three carefully.
questions: What proportion of the overall plan is represented by road autonomy?
Where is the primary concentration risk in this business model?

units.title: AD0 · What it is (spoken, slide 08)
units.body: A replacement rear-view mirror with a display built in, four small body cameras and a loom. Fifty thousand rupees, fitted in an afternoon. It is the least sophisticated thing we make and it ships first, on current-generation hardware.
questions: What hardware components are included in the AD0 product package?
What is the retail price and installation timeline for AD0?

units.title: AD0 · How it works (spoken, slide 09)
units.body: Four cameras cover the quarters a driver cannot see. The chip stitches them into a single surround view and watches the danger zone for anything entering it. The driver gets a stitched image and a directional chime. No braking, no steering — it informs, and that is the whole product.
questions: How does the AD0 system process camera feeds and alert the driver?
Does AD0 take active control of vehicle steering or braking?

units.title: AD0 · Who buys it (spoken, slide 10)
units.body: No mandate applies here, which is exactly the point: it already sells on its own merits. Owners and small fleets buy it as an accessory, through fitment shops and accessory catalogues, for visibility and parking. Demand does not wait for a compliance date.
questions: How does AD0 sell without any regulatory mandates forcing adoption?
Who is the target customer purchasing the AD0 product?

units.title: AD0 · How it fits (spoken, slide 11)
units.body: Two hundred and seventy crore, twenty-four percent of group revenue, at eighty-nine percent gross margin. It carries the highest unit count of anything in the portfolio and the lowest fitment complexity — so it builds the channel reach that the harder products inherit later.
questions: What is the revenue contribution and gross margin for AD0?
How does AD0 help build channel reach for subsequent products?

units.title: AD1 · What it is (spoken, slide 12)
units.body: A self-driving retrofit kit for vehicles that never leave a building: a sensor head, a compute box, and a drive-by-wire interface. One lakh rupees. Fitted to forklifts and tugs a site already owns.
questions: What does the AD1 retrofit kit cost and consist of?
Can AD1 be installed on existing forklifts and tugs?
How much does the indoor autonomous kit cost?
What hardware is included in the AD1 self-driving kit?

units.title: AD1 · How it works (spoken, slide 13)
units.body: This is the first product where the silicon closes the loop instead of advising. Cameras and depth sensing read the aisle, the load and the people in it. The chip localises against a site map it holds onboard. A planner picks a path and a speed. Then drive-by-wire actually steers, accelerates and brakes. The vehicle drives; the driver is not there.
questions: How does AD1 handle navigation without a driver?
What enables the vehicle to steer and brake autonomously in AD1?
Does AD1 rely on cloud processing or onboard silicon?
How does the system close the loop instead of just advising?

units.title: AD1 · Who buys it (spoken, slide 14)
units.body: Warehouse and industrial operators, direct or through material-handling integrators. Inside a private site no homologation applies, so this is a commercial decision, not a regulatory one — which is why level-four behaviour ships here years before it is legal on a public road.
questions: Who are the target buyers for the AD1 product?
Why can AD1 deploy years before public road autonomous vehicles?
Does selling AD1 require regulatory homologation or government approvals?
How do industrial operators and material-handling integrators purchase this?

units.title: AD1 · How it fits (spoken, slide 15)
units.body: Forty-two crore, under four percent of revenue. Small in the model and large in the argument: it is the technical proof point for the road roadmap, running the same silicon in a place where it is allowed to make the decision.
questions: What is AD1's financial contribution to overall revenue?
Why is a relatively small revenue contributor strategically important for the roadmap?
How much does AD1 generate in revenue?

units.title: AD1 · Proven in a simulator (spoken, slide 16)

units.body: And this is what the customer is actually buying, running. units.title: D-HUMR · Proven in a simulator (spoken, slide 75)
units.body: A live perimeter console. units.title: D100 drone · How it works (spoken, slide 78)
units.body: Cameras and an inertial unit read the scene and the airframe's own motion. The chip holds position and detects obstacles onboard, so the aircraft is not dependent on a radio link to stay safe. The flight controller executes.
questions: How does the D100 drone maintain position and detect obstacles without a radio link?
What hardware components are used for perception and motion tracking on the D100?
How does the flight controller interact with onboard compute to keep the aircraft safe?

units.title: D100 drone · Who buys it (spoken, slide 79)
units.body: Airframe builders with onboard autonomy requirements — inspection, survey, and any mission flown where the radio link cannot be relied upon. They buy compute, not aircraft, and they build the rest themselves.
questions: What kind of customers buy the D100 compute kit and what do they use it for?
Why do airframe builders buy compute instead of complete aircraft from us?
How does the D100 handle missions where radio links are unreliable?

units.title: D100 drone · How it fits (spoken, slide 80)
units.body: Twenty crore. Treat it as optionality rather than base case: the same die, in a market with a different cycle and different buyers, entered without designing new silicon to get there.
questions: What is the projected revenue contribution of the D100 drone product?
Should investors view the D100 as a core base case or just optionality?
Did entering this new market require designing a brand new silicon chip?

units.title: Part five — Portfolio economics (spoken, slide 81)
units.body: Fifteen products explained. Now what they do together — concentration, timing, where the autonomy actually runs, where the margin is, and how much of each market we are assuming we win.
questions: What topics are covered in the portfolio economics section after explaining the fifteen products?
How do the portfolio products interact regarding concentration, timing, and margin?
What market share assumptions are baked into the portfolio economics?

units.title: Concentration (spoken, slide 82)
units.body: Be clear about this: two SKUs carry sixty-four percent. The truck kit and the smart mirror are the same product family sold to overlapping buyers, so a certification delay or an installation bottleneck hits seven hundred and twenty crore at once — more than the other thirteen SKUs combined. That is the single largest risk in the plan.
questions: What is the single biggest concentration risk in the portfolio?
How much revenue depends on the truck kit and the smart mirror?
Why are certification delays or installation bottlenecks such a catastrophic threat to 720 crore of revenue?
Aren't the truck kit and smart mirror just the same product disguised as two SKUs?

units.title: Sequencing (spoken, slide 83)
units.body: Six SKUs earn revenue in the 2027 financial year, nine more in 2028. The 2027 revenue is one point seven crore across six products, on current-generation hardware — deliberately small. The ramp switches on when production silicon reaches market, and the licence line starts later still. The shape of this plan is gated by the chip, which is what the round funds.
questions: What is the revenue timeline for the SKUs across 2027 and 2028?
Why is the 2027 revenue so tiny at just 1.7 crore?
Is this entire business plan just waiting around for production silicon?
When do the license revenues actually kick in?

units.title: Where autonomy runs (spoken, slide 84)
units.body: Eighty-six percent of revenue runs outdoors, where public-road rules and homologation apply.
