Six percent runs indoors, geofenced, where level four ships years earlier on identical silicon. Eight percent is pure compute with no vehicle exposure at all. Same chip, three very different regulatory positions.
questions: How is the revenue split between outdoor, indoor, and pure compute applications?
Why does indoor autonomy ship years earlier than outdoor public-road systems?
What regulatory hurdles apply to the eighty-six percent of revenue running outdoors?

units.title: Margin (spoken, slide 85)
units.body: Volume and margin sit in different places, and that is the useful thing on this slide. Systems are eighty-three percent of revenue, so group economics track systems. But the marginal rupee is worth most in semiconductors at ninety-four percent, and those lines need no installation capacity. Growth in the silicon SKUs improves group margin without adding operational load.
questions: Which product lines drive the group margins and volume?
Why are semiconductor SKUs so much more valuable on the margin?
Does growth in the silicon SKUs add operational or installation headaches?

units.title: Headroom (spoken, slide 86)
units.body: No SKU in this plan assumes we win its market. Every line sits under two percent of its own sized demand pool, and most pools are global while our addressable market is the India slice — so the real share is higher than shown. Read the port line differently: that pool is total port automation, and we sell only the vehicle layer.
questions: What percentage of the addressable market does each SKU assume we capture?
How does the model calculate market share when port automation is mentioned?
Is this plan banking on capturing dominant market shares?
How realistic is the volume assumption relative to total market size?

units.title: The ask (spoken, slide 87)
units.body: Fifteen products, one tapeout. The demand is legislated, the margin sits in silicon that needs no installation capacity, and no line in the plan requires us to win its market. Release the capital against silicon, certification and paying customers — not against the forecast. The portfolio is not fifteen bets. It is one bet, fifteen times over.
questions: What is the core thesis of this funding round?
What are investors actually releasing capital for in this round?
Is this portfolio fifteen distinct bets or just one underlying gamble on silicon?

units.title: Cover (spoken, slide 01)
units.body: DeepGrid Semi. Fifteen product SKUs, built on one chip. This is where our eleven hundred and twenty-eight crore revenue plan comes from, and why the decision in front of you is simpler than a fifteen-product portfolio makes it look.
questions: What is DeepGrid Semi's overall revenue target for this plan?
How many product SKUs are built on the single chip?
Why should investors view this as a simple decision instead of a complex fifteen-product portfolio?

units.title: The case (spoken, slide 02)
units.body: Our portfolio is a consequence of the silicon, not a strategy you have to believe fifteen times over. Every SKU runs the same twenty-eight nanometre chip under different firmware. Two SKUs carry sixty-four percent of the plan, and every line sits under two percent of its own demand pool.
questions: What underlies all fifteen SKUs in the portfolio?
What percentage of the revenue plan is concentrated in just two SKUs?
Is this product strategy just a diversified illusion backed by the exact same chip?

units.title: Why now (spoken, slide 03)
units.body: India now requires drowsiness, blind-spot and lane-departure systems on commercial vehicles. New models from April twenty-twenty-six, the existing fleet from October. That is a pool of one million trucks a year that must comply. The buying decision is when, not whether.
questions: What new regulatory mandates are driving commercial vehicle safety in India?
When do commercial vehicle fleets have to comply with drowsiness and lane-departure requirements?
How large is the annual addressation pool for compliant commercial trucks?

units.title: The gap (spoken, slide 04)
units.body: Today that obligation is met with imported compute costing three to eight thousand dollars a module. Our die costs three dollars and eighty-eight cents at volume. Read that honestly — a bare die is not a finished module — but the gap is the opening, and it is why a locally designed part can be priced for this market.
questions: How much do imported compute modules currently cost compared to our die?
What is the actual manufacturing cost of our bare die at volume?
Are we being realistic by comparing a bare three-dollar die to an expensive imported module?

units.title: The move (spoken, slide 05)
units.body: The round funds one thing: a phased twenty-eight nanometre programme. Three point one seven million dollars, in four gated stages. We prove the compute and radar blocks on a shared wafer, then the full die, and we commit to the production mask only once silicon works.
questions: What is the exact use of proceeds for this funding round?
How much capital is being raised and how is the 28nm program structured?
At what point do you commit to the production mask?
Is this financing burning cash on multiple unproven bets or a single phased program?

units.title: The portfolio (spoken, slide 06)
units.body: Fifteen SKUs across four platform surfaces. Prices run from five thousand rupees for the driver-monitor wearable to one crore for the perception licence. Same silicon underneath all of it, priced independently by the market each one serves.
questions: How many SKUs and platform surfaces make up the portfolio?
What is the spread in pricing across your product lineup?
Are you using custom silicon for each product or the same underlying chip?
Why should we believe wildly different market segments will accept such a massive variance in pricing?

units.title: Concentration (spoken, slide 07)
units.body: Two SKUs carry sixty-four percent. The Smart Truck kit at four hundred and fifty crore, the Smart Mirror at two hundred and seventy. They are the same product family sold to overlapping buyers, so a certification or installation delay hits seven hundred and twenty crore at once. That single exposure is larger than the other thirteen SKUs combined.
questions: What is the revenue concentration risk in the portfolio?
How exposed is the business to delays in the Smart Truck and Smart Mirror lines?
Is it true that a single bottleneck can threaten over seven hundred crore of pipeline?

units.title: Sequencing (spoken, slide 08)
units.body: Six SKUs earn revenue in financial year twenty-seven, on FPGA hardware, totalling one point seven crore. Nine more switch on the following year as ASIC-era product reaches market, and the licence line begins in twenty-nine. The ramp is gated by silicon — which is precisely what this round pays for.
questions: What is the revenue timeline for the SKU rollout across upcoming financial years?
When do we transition from FPGA hardware to ASIC-era products?
Isn't this revenue ramp overly dependent on silicon milestones that always slip?

units.title: Where autonomy runs (spoken, slide 09)
units.body: The same chip operates in three domains. Outdoor carries eighty-six percent of revenue and depends on homologation and public-road rules. Indoor is geofenced, so level-four behaviour ships years earlier. Compute carries no vehicle exposure at all — it is silicon sold as silicon.
questions: Across how many operational domains does the same chip run?
What percentage of revenue relies on outdoor homologation and public-road regulations?
How does the compute domain insulate the business from vehicle exposure?

units.title: Road autonomy (spoken, slide 10)
units.body: Three kits, seven hundred and sixty-two crore, eighty-nine percent gross margin. The Smart Mirror is the entry product and the volume ramp. The Smart Truck kit is the mandated core. The indoor level-four kit removes traffic and homologation from the problem entirely.
questions: What are the financials and margins for the road autonomy kits?
Which product drives the volume ramp versus the mandated core?
How does the indoor level-four kit sidestep homologation hurdles?

units.title: Smart Mirror (spoken, slide 11)
units.body: Fifty-four thousand units by twenty-thirty-two at fifty thousand rupees, giving two hundred and seventy crore. This one is not mandated — it is a voluntary safety and convenience purchase in a market already worth three point one billion dollars, where Maruti and Tata are fitting surround-view today. What has to be true is channel reach, price holding, and the existing sales base being real.
questions: What are the unit economics and volume projections for the Smart Mirror through 2032?
Is the Smart Mirror a mandated purchase or a discretionary add-on?
What market assumptions have to hold true for the Smart Mirror targets to be realistic?

units.title: Smart Truck (spoken, slide 12)
units.body: Eighteen thousand units at two and a half lakh, giving four hundred and fifty crore — the largest SKU in the plan. It answers a legal obligation on N2 and N3 vehicles, so the buyer does not need persuading that safety is worth paying for. Three things must land: certification through ARAI or ICAT, installation capacity at scale, and fleet access.
questions: What drives the demand for the Smart Truck kit?
What are the critical execution risks for capturing the Smart Truck market?
How can you assume fleet buyers won't push back on pricing just because it's legally mandated?

units.title: Selling the chip, part one (spoken, slide 13)
units.body: The highest-margin revenue we have. The bare die sold to other manufacturers at ninety-four percent gross margin, needing no integration, certification or installation. Alongside it, the entry and mid compute modules — the cheapest way for a customer to adopt the silicon.
questions: What are the margins on bare die sales to third-party manufacturers?
Why do bare die sales require zero integration or certification overhead?
What entry and mid compute modules are available for silicon adoption?

units.title: Selling the chip, part two (spoken, slide 14)
units.body: The four-channel PCIe card is our highest-priced compute SKU at three lakh, and the closest the module line comes to a full system. The perception licence carries fifty crore on pure margin — but it has no separately sized demand pool behind it, so treat it as optionality rather than base case.
questions: What is the pricing and positioning of the four-channel PCIe card?
How much revenue is attributed to the perception licence and should we count on it?
Isn't the perception licence just wishful thinking if there is no sized demand pool behind it?

units.title: Fleet and mobility (spoken, slide 15)
units.body: Two service-model lines with the highest revenue per unit in the portfolio. Autonomous transport-as-a-service at sixty-six lakh a vehicle, debt-financed against the trucks rather than funded from equity. And port autonomy, where we already hold a live order at Vizag Container Terminal.
questions: What is the revenue per unit for autonomous transport-as-a-service?
How is the autonomous truck fleet financed?
Where is the live order for port autonomy currently held?
Which product lines generate the highest revenue per unit in the portfolio?
Are the autonomous trucks funded through equity or debt?

units.title: Sensors, part one (spoken, slide 16)
units.body: Fifty percent gross margin — the lowest in the portfolio, and we state that plainly. Thermal and radar are carried for capability: Indian night and fog are exactly where camera-only systems fail. The driver-monitor wearable at five thousand rupees is the easiest first purchase a fleet can make.
questions: Why carry thermal and radar sensors if they have the lowest gross margin in the portfolio?
What is the gross margin for the sensor products?
How do you justify keeping a product line with a fifty percent gross margin?
What is the price point of the driver-monitor wearable?
Why do camera-only systems fail in Indian operating conditions?

units.title: Sensors, part two (spoken, slide 17)
units.body: The defence ground vehicle is the only line in this deck with revenue already received — one crore, from the Army, on FPGA hardware. The drone kit opens a second procurement cycle for very little incremental engineering, because it runs the same perception and compute.
questions: Which product line has actually generated revenue received to date?
How much revenue has the defence ground vehicle line received from the Army?
What hardware does the defence ground vehicle run on?
Why does the drone kit require very little incremental engineering?
Is there any actual revenue in this deck or are these just projections?

units.title: Margin (spoken, slide 18)
units.body: Volume and margin sit in different places. Systems are eighty-three percent of revenue at eighty-nine percent margin, so group economics track that line. But the marginal rupee is worth most in semiconductors at ninety-four percent, and those SKUs need no installation capacity at all.
questions: Where do volume and margin sit within the business?
What percentage of revenue do systems represent and what is their margin?
Which segment offers the highest marginal rupee return?
Why do semiconductor SKUs not require installation capacity?
How do group economics track against the product lines?

units.title: Headroom (spoken, slide 19)
units.body: No SKU in this plan assumes we win its market. Every line with a sized pool sits under two percent of it, and most of those pools are global while our serviceable market is the India slice. These are floors, not stretches.
questions: What market share do your financial projections assume?
Are these addressable market claims realistic or inflated?
What percentage of the addressable market do your SKUs target?
Are the market size pools global or restricted to India?
Should we treat these revenue projections as stretched targets or conservative floors?

units.title: The ask (spoken, slide 20)
units.body: Fund the silicon, and the portfolio follows. Fifteen SKUs, one tapeout. We would rather be measured against verifiable gates — working silicon, certification achieved, and pilots converted to paying customers — than against a terminal-year forecast. The portfolio is not fifteen bets. It is one bet, fifteen times over.
questions: What are you actually asking us to fund with this round?
How many SKUs are tied to this single tapeout?
What milestones and verifiable gates will management be measured against?
Why should we trust terminal-year forecasts if the portfolio is just fifteen bets on one silicon design?
What does funding the silicon actually entail for the rest of the portfolio?

units.title: Cover (spoken, slide 01)
units.body: DeepGrid Semi. A walkthrough of our financial plan, prepared for a pre-Series A raise of forty-five crore in equity alongside a ten crore collateral-free debt facility. Every figure you will see is a management projection, not a reported result.
questions: How much capital is DeepGrid Semi trying to raise in this pre-Series A round?
What is the breakdown between equity and debt for this fundraising?
Are the financial figures in this dossier verified results or just management projections?
What is the size of the collateral-free debt facility being sought?
Who prepared this financial plan walkthrough?

units.title: Executive summary (spoken, slide 02)
units.body: The plan reaches self-funding on this round. One twenty-eight nanometre chip serves four markets. Revenue is projected at eleven hundred and twenty-eight crore by financial year thirty-two, at a thirty-four point four percent EBITDA margin. We turn EBITDA-positive in twenty-twenty-eight, a full year before the projected cash low point of ten point one crore.
questions: When does the company reach self-funding status based on this plan?
What is the projected revenue by financial year thirty-two?
What EBITDA margin is projected for the business?
When does the company turn EBITDA-positive and when does it hit its cash low point?
How many markets does the 128-nanometre chip serve?

units.title: The ask (spoken, slide 03)
units.body: Forty-five crore of equity at a two hundred and four crore pre-money valuation, giving an investor eighteen point zero seven percent. Alongside it, a ten crore CGTMSE-backed facility. The structure is deliberate: equity funds the silicon, debt funds the working-capital cycle.
questions: What is the pre-money valuation for this equity raise?
What equity stake does the forty-five crore investment purchase?
What is the purpose of the CGTMSE-backed facility?
Why is the funding split between equity and debt instead of using equity for everything?
What specific use of funds is allocated to the silicon versus working capital?

units.title: Market (spoken, slide 04)
units.body: Indian regulation converts advanced driver assistance from an optional purchase into a required one. Around one million commercial vehicles a year fall in scope — half a million new build, half a million retrofit. Our plan captures one point eight percent of that pool.
questions: How does Indian regulation impact the adoption of advanced driver assistance systems?
What is the total addressable size of the commercial vehicle market in scope annually?
What market share percentage does your plan actually capture?
What proportion of the target commercial vehicle market consists of retrofits versus new builds?
Is this regulatory tailwind enough to guarantee your volume assumptions?

units.title: Platform (spoken, slide 05)
units.body: The same chip and the same software stack ship under different firmware across road autonomy, silicon and compute, fleet, and sensors and robotics. That is why one tapeout can support four revenue lines rather than four separate engineering programmes.
questions: How does a single tapeout support multiple markets?
What prevents you from needing separate engineering programmes for each vertical?
Is the hardware identical across different verticals like robotics and autonomy?

units.title: Part one: the revenue plan (spoken, slide 06)
units.body: First, how volume, price and customer count build to the projection.
questions: How are volume, price, and customer count derived in the forecast?
What components make up the revenue projection build?

units.title: Revenue (spoken, slide 07)
units.body: Revenue is built bottom-up: every line is units multiplied by price. No total is set as a target and back-solved. The plan runs from one point seven crore to eleven hundred and twenty-eight crore across six years, with the inflection in twenty-twenty-eight.
questions: Are the revenue targets back-solved from a top-down goal?
What is the revenue growth trajectory over the six-year plan?
When does the revenue inflection point happen?
What are the starting and ending revenue figures in the forecast?

units.title: Revenue mix (spoken, slide 08)
units.body: Road autonomy carries two-thirds of the projection. That concentration is deliberate, because mandated demand is the largest and most predictable pool — but it also means the two truck and mirror ramps are the assumptions that most affect the outcome.
questions: How concentrated is the revenue in road autonomy?
Why rely so heavily on road autonomy instead of diversifying?
Which specific product ramps have the most impact on the financial outcome?

units.title: Business mix (spoken, slide 09)
units.body: Systems, not standalone chip sales, are the economic engine — eighty-three percent of projected revenue. The silicon creates the cost advantage; the revenue is realised by selling complete, certified systems built around it.
questions: Are you selling standalone chips or complete systems?
What drives the majority of the projected revenue?
How does the silicon create a financial advantage if systems drive the revenue?

units.title: Unit economics (spoken, slide 10)
units.body: Eleven product lines, each priced independently. Prices are held flat across the plan, so growth comes from volume rather than from price increases. The truck kit and the smart mirror together represent seven hundred and twenty crore.
questions: How many product lines do you have and how are they priced?
Does growth rely on raising prices over time?
What is the combined revenue contribution of the truck kit and smart mirror?

units.title: Customers (spoken, slide 11)
units.body: Accounts grow from five to six hundred and fifty. Average revenue per account peaks in twenty-twenty-nine and then falls as the base broadens into retrofit and fleet channels — which is what removes single-account dependency from the plan.
questions: How does the customer count scale over the forecast period?
Why does average revenue per account eventually decline?
How do you address single-account dependency as the business scales?

units.title: Part two: margin and profitability (spoken, slide 12)
units.body: Next, how gross margin expands and overhead ratios decline.
questions: How do gross margins expand over the forecast period?
What is the trajectory for overhead ratios?

units.title: Margin architecture (spoken, slide 13)
units.body: Each segment carries its own margin path. The blended margin is an output of the mix, not an assumption applied to the top line. The expansion comes from the chip displacing a bought-in module inside every kit.
questions: How is the blended gross margin calculated?
What drives the gross margin expansion over time?
Are you just assuming gross margin improvements or is there a structural driver?

units.title: Profit and loss (spoken, slide 14)
units.body: Revenue, gross profit and every expense line derive from the same build. Gross margin rises from thirty-nine point seven percent to eighty-seven point four. EBITDA turns positive in twenty-twenty-eight and reaches three hundred and eighty-eight crore by thirty-two.
questions: How does gross margin improve across the forecast?
When does the company reach positive EBITDA and what is the peak?
Is the P&L built from the same assumptions as the revenue plan?

units.title: Operating leverage (spoken, slide 15)
units.body: The step from loss to structural profitability happens once revenue clears the fixed engineering base. Net margin reaches twenty-four point three percent in the terminal year.
questions: When does the company transition from burning cash to sustainable profitability?
What is the projected net profit margin by the final year?
At what revenue threshold does operating leverage kick in?
Is this projected profitability actually structural or just a temporary spike?

units.title: Cost discipline (spoken, slide 16)
units.body: All three overhead ratios decline as revenue scales. Research and development stays high by design at thirty-three percent, because it carries the next silicon generation rather than only sustaining the current one.
questions: How do overhead costs behave as top-line revenue scales?
Why is the R&D burn rate remaining so high at thirty-three percent?
Is the high R&D spend just maintaining legacy products or building future tech?

units.title: Research investment (spoken, slide 17)
units.body: About three hundred crore of cumulative research spending funds the next five-nanometre chip from operating profit. Read this correctly: that spending is an expense inside the projections you have seen, not an addition to them.
questions: How much cumulative R&D capital is required to fund the next-gen 5nm chip?
Is the 5nm R&D budget already baked into the financial projections or is it an uncounted add-on?
Where is the funding for the next silicon generation coming from?

units.title: Part three: silicon and capital (spoken, slide 18)
units.body: Now what the round funds, what the chip costs, and when it pays back.
questions: What is this funding round actually going to pay for?
What are the unit economics of the new chip and what is the payback timeline?

units.title: Use of funds (spoken, slide 19)
units.body: Fifty-five crore in total. Silicon takes fifty-four percent, and equals sixty-six percent of the equity round on its own. Working capital sits on the facility, not on equity.
questions: What is the total capital requirement for this round?
How much of the equity round is being consumed directly by the silicon programme?
How is working capital being financed if not through equity?

units.title: Silicon programme (spoken, slide 20)
units.body: The tapeout is phased so the largest commitment comes last. Blocks are proven on shared wafers first; the production mask is ordered only once silicon works. Most of the spend is gated on evidence rather than on schedule.
questions: What is the risk mitigation strategy for the tapeout schedule?
Are you blindly burning cash on a fixed schedule or gating R&D spend on actual milestones?
How are the chip blocks tested before ordering the expensive production mask?

units.title: Chip economics (spoken, slide 21)
units.body: At volume the die costs three dollars eighty-eight, derived from die size, wafer price and yield. The programme recovers its one-time cost at about a hundred and seventy-five thousand chips, well inside the plan horizon.
questions: What is the fully loaded unit cost per die at volume?
How many units need to ship before the chip development costs are fully recovered?
Is the breakeven volume realistic within the current strategic plan horizon?

units.title: Schedule risk (spoken, slide 22)
units.body: If the next-generation chip slips twelve months, the plan loses about fifty-eight crore in the terminal year. The mandated truck and mirror business is unaffected, because it runs on current-generation silicon.
questions: What is the financial impact if the next-generation chip roadmap slips by a year?
Does a delay in the new silicon jeopardize our existing truck and mirror revenue streams?
How insulated is current-generation revenue from next-gen R&D delays?

units.title: Cash and runway (spoken, slide 23)
units.body: Cash falls to a low point of ten point one crore in twenty-twenty-nine, then recovers as silicon spending completes and operating profit outpaces working-capital growth. No further equity round is assumed.
questions: How low does cash reserves drop before the business starts generating positive free cash flow?
When does the cash trough occur and what causes the subsequent recovery?
Are you certain we won't need to come back to investors for another dilutive equity round?

units.title: Capital structure (spoken, slide 24)
units.body: Equity funds the asset; debt funds the cycle. Indian commercial-vehicle customers settle in sixty to ninety days, and working capital absorbs eighty crore in the terminal year alone — a cost that should not consume equity.
questions: How is the working capital cycle being financed?
Why are we relying on debt instead of equity to fund working capital needs?
How are slow-paying commercial vehicle customers impacting our cash requirements in the terminal year?

units.title: Ownership and prior capital (spoken, slide 25)
units.body: The company is founder-controlled, with two point four eight crore of grant and angel capital already deployed. For an incoming investor, governance rights matter more here than the ownership percentage.
questions: Who currently controls the company?
How much angel and grant money has already been spent?
Should an incoming investor care more about equity stake or governance rights here?
Is this company founder-controlled or already institutionalized?

units.title: Operating plan (spoken, slide 26)
units.body: Headcount grows from thirty-four to five hundred and forty-one, weighted to engineering. We present it as the operating shape of the plan, and we reconcile it to the expense ratios before close rather than merging the two now.
questions: How many employees are you planning to hire, and what roles are prioritized?
Why aren't headcount projections reconciled with expense ratios right now?
What is the projected headcount growth in the operating plan?

units.title: Part four: risk and decision (spoken, slide 27)
units.body: Finally, the downside cases and what happens next.
questions: What is covered in the final section of the presentation?

units.title: Scenarios (spoken, slide 28)
units.body: Each case is driven by one revenue multiplier and one overhead adjustment, so the downside is testable rather than asserted. Even on a seventy percent revenue miss, the plan self-funds without a further equity round.
questions: What happens to the cash runway if revenues miss projections by seventy percent?
Will the company need another equity round if the downside scenario plays out?
How are the financial scenarios modeled and tested?

units.title: What determines the outcome (spoken, slide 29)
units.body: Five assumptions carry the projection: the two unit ramps, systems gross margin, yield and wafer cost, working-capital intensity, and the silicon schedule. Against each, we are assembling the evidence a diligence team would ask for.
questions: Which core assumptions drive the financial projections?
What evidence is being prepared for the diligence team?

units.title: Close (spoken, slide 30)
units.body: We are raising forty-five crore to fund working silicon, paired with a ten crore non-dilutive facility, against a plan that reaches self-funding without a further round. We would rather be measured on verifiable gates — working silicon, certification, and paying customers — than on the terminal year.
questions: How much capital are you raising and what is the debt component?
What verifiable milestones should investors judge this company on instead of terminal year forecasts?
Does this financing round get the company to self-funding without needing more equity?

units.title: Cover (spoken)
units.body: Fifteen products. One chip. This is the long version — every SKU in the plan, what it physically is, how it runs on shared silicon, who pays for it, and what it contributes. Everything here is a management projection prepared for fundraising.
questions: Are these numbers audited historical results or just management forecasts?
What is actually in this fundraising deck?
How many products and chips are being pitched here?

units.title: How to read this deck (spoken)
units.body: Each product gets the same four slides, in the same order: what it is, how it works, who buys it and why now, and how it fits. Four of them get two more, because a working simulator exists and you should watch it rather than take our word. Learn the pattern once and the next eighty slides navigate themselves.
questions: Is every product presented using the same slide structure?
Which products have a working simulator you can actually watch?
How is this massive deck organized for an analyst to read?

units.title: Why now (spoken)
units.body: The demand is legislated, not forecast. Driver-drowsiness, blind-spot and lane-departure obligations land on new and existing commercial vehicles on fixed dates. About a million trucks a year fall in scope. For a fleet operator the question is not whether to buy — it is whose chip is inside when they do.
questions: Is customer demand driven by actual legislation or just optimistic market forecasts?
How large is the addressable fleet market in terms of trucks per year?
Why are fleet operators forced to buy these chips now?

units.title: The move (spoken)
units.body: The whole plan is downstream of one 28 nanometre part, and the programme is deliberately gated. Prove the compute and radar blocks first. Then the full die. Then backend sign-off. The production mask — the largest single commitment — is only paid for once working silicon exists.
questions: What is the risk mitigation strategy for the 28nm silicon development?
When do you actually pay for the expensive production mask?
What are the major development gates before committing to full production?

units.title: The silicon (spoken)
units.body: Here is the part itself. Thirty-two thousand seven hundred and sixty-eight multiply-accumulate units at six hundred megahertz, a hundred and two gigabytes a second of memory bandwidth, hardware softmax, and lockstep cores for the automotive safety path. The number that matters most: it fuses eleven sensor channels in eight point six milliseconds of a thirty-three millisecond frame. Seventy-four percent of the frame is left unused, and that headroom is why one die becomes fifteen products.
questions: What are the core technical specifications of the custom silicon?
How fast does the chip process multi-sensor fusion per frame?
Why does a single die support fifteen different end products?
Does the processor handle safety-critical automotive workloads?

units.title: The portfolio (spoken)
units.body: All fifteen, ranked by revenue in the final year. Prices are held flat across six years, so growth comes from volume, not from price. Note how far the list ranges — fifty thousand rupees for a mirror unit, eighteen thousand for a bare die, several lakh for a truck kit. Same silicon, priced independently by the market it sells into.
questions: How does revenue scale across the fifteen product variants?
Are financial projections driven by price hikes or volume growth?
What is the price range across the product portfolio?
How can the exact same silicon command such wildly different market prices?

units.title: Part one — Road autonomy (spoken)
units.body: Road autonomy is two-thirds of the plan: seven hundred and sixty-two crore, three SKUs. This is where the mandate acts, and where the concentration risk sits. Take these three carefully.
questions: What percentage of the business plan is dedicated to road autonomy?
Where is the primary concentration risk for the company located?
How many SKUs are tied to the road autonomy strategy?

units.title: AD0 · What it is (spoken)
units.body: A replacement rear-view mirror with a display built in, four small body cameras and a loom. Fifty thousand rupees, fitted in an afternoon. It is the least sophisticated thing we make and it ships first, on current-generation hardware.
questions: What are the physical components of the AD0 product?
How much does the AD0 rear-view mirror system cost?
Does AD0 require next-generation hardware to operate?

units.title: AD0 · How it works (spoken)
units.body: Four cameras cover the quarters a driver cannot see. The chip stitches them into a single surround view and watches the danger zone for anything entering it. The driver gets a stitched image and a directional chime. No braking, no steering — it informs, and that is the whole product.
questions: Does the AD0 system take active control of braking and steering?
What specific functions does the AD0 safety feature perform?
How many cameras feed into the AD0 surround-view display?

units.title: AD0 · Who buys it (spoken)
units.body: No mandate applies here, which is exactly the point: it already sells on its own merits. Owners and small fleets buy it as an accessory, through fitment shops and accessory catalogues, for visibility and parking. Demand does not wait for a compliance date.
questions: Are AD0 sales dependent on government safety mandates?
Who is actually buying and installing the AD0 aftermarket mirror?
How is AD0 distributed to end customers without a regulatory push?

units.title: AD0 · How it fits (spoken)
units.body: Two hundred and seventy crore, twenty-four percent of group revenue, at eighty-nine percent gross margin. It carries the highest unit count of anything in the portfolio and the lowest fitment complexity — so it builds the channel reach that the harder products inherit later.
questions: What share of total group revenue comes from AD0?
What is the gross margin on the AD0 mirror product?
Why is AD0 considered crucial for building out the broader sales channel?

units.title: AD1 · What it is (spoken)
units.body: A self-driving retrofit kit for vehicles that never leave a building: a sensor head, a compute box, and a drive-by-wire interface. One lakh rupees. Fitted to forklifts and tugs a site already owns.
questions: What is included in the AD1 self-driving retrofit package?
What types of industrial vehicles are targeted by AD1?
How much does the AD1 kit cost?

units.title: AD1 · How it works (spoken)
units.body: This is the first product where the silicon closes the loop instead of advising. Cameras and depth sensing read the aisle, the load and the people in it. The chip localises against a site map it holds onboard. A planner picks a path and a speed. Then drive-by-wire actually steers, accelerates and brakes. The vehicle drives; the driver is not there.
questions: How does AD1 achieve autonomous navigation in industrial settings?
Does AD1 take control of vehicle steering and braking?
Is there an operator inside the vehicle when AD1 is active?

units.title: AD1 · Who buys it (spoken)
units.body: Warehouse and industrial operators, direct or through material-handling integrators. Inside a private site no homologation applies, so this is a commercial decision, not a regulatory one — which is why level-four behaviour ships here years before it is legal on a public road.
questions: Who purchases the AD1 warehouse automation kits?
Why can level-four autonomy ship in warehouses before public roads?
Are industrial retrofit sales subject to public road homologation delays?

units.title: AD1 · How it fits (spoken)
units.body: Forty-two crore, under four percent of revenue. Small in the model and large in the argument: it is the technical proof point for the road roadmap, running the same silicon in a place where it is allowed to make the decision.
questions: How much does the AD1 project cost and what proportion of revenue does it represent?
Why is such a small revenue contributor considered strategically important?
Is AD1 just an expensive vanity project or does it actually prove anything?
What is the financial scale of AD1 relative to overall revenue?

units.title: AD1 · Proven in a simulator (spoken)
units.body: We built a drawable warehouse floor for this. You author the route, place workers, peer vehicles, trolleys and spills as obstacles, and run it. The alert policy is configurable — honk, voice, both, silent — because that is a site decision, not ours. And recovery is explicit: it reroutes after a set stuck-time.
questions: How was the AD1 warehouse simulator built and what features does it include?
Can warehouse operators customize the alert and recovery policies in the simulation?
How does the simulator handle vehicle rerouting when obstacles block a path?

units.title: AD1 · The simulator, running (spoken)
units.body: Here it is, actually running. Inbound put-away, then a pick run, then the peak-hour floor. Watch the safety ring travelling with the truck and gating its speed, and watch the sensor-fusion panel top right build the bird's-eye view. The third scenario is the one that decides whether a site can run this.
questions: What key safety features are visible when running the AD1 warehouse simulator?
Which specific scenario in the simulation determines whether a site can adopt the system?
How does the sensor-fusion panel function during live simulation runs?

units.title: AD2 · What it is (spoken)
units.body: The Smart Truck kit — forward camera, radar, compute box, driver display and the harness that talks to the vehicle. Two and a half lakh rupees. This is the biggest single line in the plan and the one the mandate is written for.
questions: What hardware components are included in the Smart Truck AD2 kit?
How much does the AD2 hardware kit cost per unit?
Why is the Smart Truck kit considered the most critical line in the entire business plan?

units.title: AD2 · How it works (spoken)
units.body: Camera and radar watch the forward path and the blind quarters. The chip fuses both into one object list carrying range and closing speed. Collision, lane and blind-spot logic decide whether to warn. The driver is warned, and where the vehicle supports it, the brake interface is signalled. Radar matters here because closing speed is what a braking decision actually turns on.
questions: How do the camera and radar sensors work together in the AD2 safety system?
Why is radar essential for making braking decisions in the AD2 kit?
How does the system warn drivers and interface with vehicle brakes?

units.title: AD2 · Who buys it (spoken)
units.body: Fleet operators and truck manufacturers, and the decision is compliance-led rather than discretionary. Retrofit through installers now; factory-fit is the longer, larger route. The buying question is which supplier, on what date.
questions: Who are the primary target buyers for the AD2 Smart Truck kit?
Is the purchase of AD2 driven by regulatory compliance or discretionary budgets?
What is the difference between the retrofit and factory-fit sales channels for this product?

units.title: AD2 · How it fits (spoken)
units.body: Four hundred and fifty crore — forty percent of group revenue from one SKU. That is the concentration to underwrite. It is also why the portfolio has a demand floor at all rather than a demand forecast.
questions: What is the revenue projection for AD2 and how concentrated is the portfolio on this single SKU?
Are we dangerously over-reliant on the AD2 product line for our revenue?
How does AD2 establish a demand floor rather than just a speculative forecast?

units.title: AD2 · Proven in a simulator (spoken)
units.body: Three road profiles — market street, single-carriageway highway, and a deliberate stress test — run against the same perception stack. The vehicle model is real: five hundred and fifty kilograms, two point one metre wheelbase, tyre friction of nought point seven five. Steering angle and lateral acceleration are solved, not scripted.
questions: What road profiles and stress tests are used in the AD2 simulator?
How realistic is the vehicle physics model used in the simulation?
Are steering angles and lateral acceleration scripted or dynamically solved in the AD2 tests?

units.title: AD2 · The simulator, running (spoken)
units.body: Watch the planner view in the centre. It redraws from the fused object list, not from an animation path. On the right, the perception rail names what it sees and how far away it is — a motorbike at twenty-six metres, an auto-rickshaw at thirty-eight. Three road profiles, one stack, nothing reloaded between them.
questions: How does the planner view in the AD2 simulator generate its path?
What information is displayed on the perception rail during a simulation run?
Do the different road profiles require reloading the perception stack?

units.title: AD2 · G · Sensor coverage (spoken)
units.body: Before we leave the truck kit, look at the sensor layout it actually ships. Two towers retrofit above the existing mirrors, each with a thermal camera, a road camera and a hundred-and-twenty-degree side camera. Two cameras in the cab. Four-D radar front and rear. Watch the coverage cones sweep and overlap — the claim the layout makes is that no quarter of a heavy truck goes unobserved.
questions: What exact sensors are included in the AD2 truck kit hardware layout?
How complete is the sensor coverage around a heavy truck equipped with this kit?
Where are the thermal, road, and side cameras physically mounted on the vehicle?

units.title: Part two — Silicon and compute (spoken)
units.body: Now the half of the business that sells the chip instead of the vehicle. A hundred and ninety-four crore across five SKUs, and the highest margins in the plan — because none of these need an installation crew.
questions: What is the revenue and margin profile of the semiconductor division?
How much revenue does the chip business generate across its SKUs?
Why does the chip business have the highest margins in the financial plan?
Do the silicon products require field installation crews?
How does the chip sales volume compare to the vehicle business?

units.title: Chipset OEM · What it is (spoken)
units.body: The bare die, in tray or reel, for a customer to place on their own board. Eighteen thousand rupees. No enclosure, no cables, no fitting — we ship silicon and a datasheet, and the customer does the rest.
questions: What is included when selling the bare die chipset OEM product?
What is the price point for the bare die chipset?
Do you supply enclosures or cables with the bare die, or just the silicon?
What deliverables are included in a bare die semiconductor shipment?

units.title: Chipset OEM · How it works (spoken)
units.body: The customer's own sensors feed their own board. Our die does the perception compute inside their design. Their software decides what to do with the result, and their product ships with our silicon inside it. We supply one stage of someone else's chain.
questions: How do customers integrate the chipset OEM product into their own hardware?
Who handles the perception compute and software decision-making in this model?
Are we selling a complete end product or just one component in someone else's supply chain?
How does the customer's sensor setup interact with our die?

units.title: Chipset OEM · Who buys it (spoken)
units.body: Manufacturers who want Indian-designed silicon and domestic supply rather than an imported part, and who have the engineering to integrate it. Procurement policy is often as decisive as specification here.
questions: Who is the target buyer for the domestic chipset OEM offering?
Why do manufacturers choose this silicon over imported alternatives?
What role does procurement policy play in selling domestic silicon?
Do buyers need internal engineering teams to use the bare die?

units.title: Chipset OEM · How it fits (spoken)
units.body: Fifty-four crore at ninety-four percent gross margin — the highest in the portfolio. Every rupee here arrives without installation capacity, warranty logistics or a fitment channel behind it.
questions: What is the revenue and gross margin contribution of the high-margin chip segment?
Why are the gross margins for this semiconductor line so exceptionally high at ninety-four percent?
Does this product line incur any installation or warranty logistics overhead?
What makes this revenue stream free from fitment channel costs?

units.title: Chipset · E · The compute (spoken)
units.body: And this is what the customer is actually buying, running. On the left, the flat eight-by-eight matrix as it works on the FPGA today: sixty-four multiply-accumulates a cycle, iterating the reduction in software. On the right, the cube on twenty-eight nanometre silicon, where that reduction becomes hardware depth and all eight layers fire at once. Watch the tile counters diverge — that gap is the eight-times figure, shown rather than claimed.
questions: How does the performance of the 28nm silicon cube compare to the FPGA implementation?
What is the actual performance speedup of the hardware reduction versus software iteration?
What is the architectural difference between the flat matrix on FPGA and the silicon cube?
How is the claimed eight-times performance improvement demonstrated?

units.title: A100 one-channel · What it is (spoken)
units.body: The same die on an M.2 module: one camera channel, plus the software kit. Sized to drop into an enclosure and a sensor the customer already owns.
questions: What is the A100 one-channel product?
What comes bundled with the M.2 module version of the die?
How does the A100 module integrate with existing customer enclosures and sensors?

units.title: A100 one-channel · How it works (spoken)
units.body: One camera in, one perception stream out, over a standard module interface. It is the smallest configuration the part supports — and the point is that it is the same part, running less.
questions: How does the A100 one-channel configuration function technically?
What are the input and output specifications for the M.2 module?
Is the A100 single-channel a separate silicon part or just a scaled-down configuration?

units.title: A100 one-channel · Who buys it (spoken)
units.body: Product teams who want the silicon and the toolchain but do not want to design a board around a bare die. It converts a semiconductor sale into a module sale for customers without a hardware team.
questions: Which customer segment buys the A100 one-channel module instead of the bare die?
How does offering an M.2 module lower the engineering barrier for customers without hardware teams?
Why would a product team choose the module over designing their own board around the silicon?

units.title: A100 one-channel · How it fits (spoken)
units.body: Twenty-five and a half crore, at eighty-nine percent margin. Modest on its own; it exists to make the silicon reachable by customers who would otherwise not buy at all.
questions: What are the revenue and margin figures for the A100 one-channel product line?
Is the A100 single-channel just a low-revenue filler product, or does it serve a strategic purpose?
How does the M.2 module expand the addressable market for the core silicon?

units.title: A100 two-channel · What it is (spoken)
units.body: A board-level module with two camera inputs and the software kit. Twenty-five thousand rupees — the middle rung of the compute-box ladder, and the one that sells in the largest numbers of the three.
questions: What is the retail price of the A100 two-channel module?
Which product tier drives the highest volume sales for the company?
What hardware comes included with the A100 two-channel board?
Is this mid-tier product actually profitable or just a volume driver?

units.title: A100 two-channel · How it works (spoken)
units.body: Two channels is where fusion begins to matter — the moment you have to reconcile two views of the same scene into one object list. It is the first configuration that justifies purpose-built transformer hardware over a general-purpose processor.
questions: Why does the two-channel configuration require purpose-built transformer hardware?
At what point do systems need sensor fusion for object reconciliation?
Does a standard general-purpose processor fall short once you move to two camera inputs?

units.title: A100 two-channel · Who buys it (spoken)
units.body: Systems that need more than a single view but not full surround coverage — reversing with side detection, a two-camera inspection rig, a small autonomous platform. Buyers who would find a four-channel card wasteful and a single channel insufficient.
questions: What are the typical use cases for the two-channel A100 module?
Which target market finds a single-channel setup insufficient but a four-channel card wasteful?
Are these two-camera rigs being deployed in small autonomous platforms?

units.title: A100 two-channel · How it fits (spoken)
units.body: Twenty-eight point eight crore. A step on a ladder rather than a destination — but the ladder is what lets one die address several price points at once.
questions: What is the total addressable market or revenue contribution of the two-channel tier?
How does having multiple rungs on the compute ladder protect margins?
Is this product line just a stepping stone or a long-term revenue anchor?

units.title: A100 four-channel · What it is (spoken)
units.body: A PCIe card carrying the chip with four camera inputs, for a host system that provides the enclosure and the power. Fifty thousand rupees, and the largest configuration we sell as a component.
questions: What are the specs and pricing for the A100 four-channel card?
Does the four-channel variant require an external enclosure and power supply from the host system?
Is this fifty-thousand-rupee component sold as a bare PCIe card?

units.title: A100 four-channel · How it works (spoken)
units.body: Four channels demands the memory bandwidth the compute geometry was designed around. Each compute cube runs its own local memory access against a banked cache, which is what keeps utilisation high instead of starving on a single shared path. This is the configuration that shows why the die is built the way it is.
questions: How does the four-channel configuration utilize memory bandwidth to prevent compute starvation?
Does the chip architecture actually justify its complex design at this scale?
Why does the banked cache architecture matter for high-utilization workloads?

units.title: A100 four-channel · Who buys it (spoken)
units.body: Customers building full surround perception who want the compute inside their own architecture rather than in a box we supply — robotics platforms, industrial vehicles, and anyone who already has a host machine and needs to add sight to it.
questions: Who actually buys the four-channel PCIe card instead of a boxed solution?
Are industrial vehicle and robotics developers integrating this directly into their own host architectures?
Why would a customer prefer adding sight to an existing machine rather than buying our enclosure?

units.title: A100 four-channel · How it fits (spoken)
units.body: Thirty-six crore, the largest of the three compute boxes. Together the A100 family is ninety crore of revenue that needs no vehicle, no installer and no homologation.
questions: What is the total revenue projection for the A100 four-channel product line?
How much total revenue does the entire A100 family generate without requiring vehicle homologation or installers?
Are these component-level sales really bypassing all vehicle integration overhead?

units.title: T100 licence · What it is (spoken)
units.body: Not hardware at all. A licence to the trained perception models and the toolchain, so a customer can run our software on their own platform. Priced per deployment, with nothing shipped in a box.
questions: How does the T100 software licence work without any physical hardware shipments?
What is the pricing model for licensing our perception models and toolchain?
Are we essentially selling pure software margins with zero hardware manufacturing costs?

units.title: T100 licence · How it works (spoken)
units.body: The models are the accumulated result of running these sensors on Indian roads. A customer licences that, integrates it, and ships. There is no board, no bill of materials, and nothing to manufacture.
questions: What proprietary value is actually embedded in the T100 licence?
How do Indian road data and trained perception models translate into licence revenue?
Can customers really integrate our models and ship without any bill of materials or board manufacturing?

units.title: T100 licence · Who buys it (spoken)
units.body: Teams that want perception tuned for Indian road conditions — the traffic mix, the lane discipline, the light — without spending three years collecting the data to train it themselves. The dataset is the product here, not the code.
questions: Who is the target customer for the T100 licence?
Why would someone buy the T100 dataset instead of building their own?
What is actually being sold with the T100 licence, the code or the data?

units.title: T100 licence · How it fits (spoken)
units.body: Fifty crore at ninety-four percent margin, and it starts later than everything else — in the 2029 financial year — because a licence needs a track record before anyone buys one. It is the only line in the plan with no bill of materials whatsoever.
questions: What are the financial projections for the T100 licence and when does it start?
Why does the T100 licence revenue only kick in during FY 2029?
Is the high-margin T100 licence just pure software with zero hardware costs?

units.title: Part three — Fleet and mobility (spoken)
units.body: Two SKUs, eighty-nine crore, and the highest revenue per unit anywhere in the portfolio. Here we stop selling a product and start selling the work the product does.
questions: What is the SKU count and revenue contribution for the fleet and mobility segment?
How does the revenue per unit in the fleet portfolio compare to the rest of the business?
Are we shifting from selling hardware to selling outcomes in this segment?

units.title: TaaS · What it is (spoken)
units.body: Not a sale. A vehicle we own and operate under contract, where the customer pays for the transport rather than the truck. The revenue per unit is the largest in the plan because we are booking the whole job.
questions: How does the TaaS business model actually work?
Why is the revenue per unit for TaaS the highest in the entire plan?
Are customers buying trucks or transport services under the TaaS model?

units.title: TaaS · How it works (spoken)
units.body: The vehicle runs the same autonomy stack as the kit we sell. Fleet logic schedules it, routes it, and hands off to a remote operator when the situation exceeds what the vehicle should decide alone. The difference from AD2 is commercial, not technical.
questions: What is the technological difference between TaaS and the AD2 kit?
How do the vehicles handle edge cases or situations requiring human intervention in TaaS?
What underlying autonomy stack powers the TaaS vehicles?

units.title: TaaS · Who buys it (spoken)
units.body: Operators comparing cost per tonne-kilometre against a driven alternative — and increasingly comparing against driver availability rather than driver cost, because on many routes the constraint is finding a driver at all.
questions: Who are the target buyers for the TaaS offering?
Are fleet operators buying TaaS to save on driver wages or because they literally cannot find drivers?
How do customers evaluate the cost-effectiveness of TaaS versus traditional transport?

units.title: TaaS · How it fits (spoken)
units.body: Sixty-six crore. It is the line that shows what the technology is worth when we capture the operating margin instead of the hardware margin. It also carries operational risk the product lines do not: we own the asset and the uptime.
questions: What is the revenue contribution allocated to TaaS in the financial plan?
What new operational risks do we take on with TaaS compared to selling standard products?
Does TaaS prove the intrinsic value of our technology by capturing operating margins?

units.title: Seaport AGV · What it is (spoken)
units.body: An autonomous container-yard vehicle working inside a port perimeter. A controlled site, but not an easy one: heavy equipment overhead, tight lanes between stacks, and real consequences for a positioning error.
questions: What is the Seaport AGV and where is it deployed?
How difficult is the operating environment for automated vehicles inside a container port?
What makes seaport container yards a challenging use case for autonomy?

units.title: Seaport AGV · How it works (spoken)
units.body: Under a quay crane, satellite positioning degrades exactly where precision matters most. Sensor fusion on our silicon holds seven centimetres in the open and twenty-two under the crane, where satellite alone falls away. That positioning is what makes crane-synchronised dispatch possible at all.
questions: How does the Seaport AGV maintain positioning accuracy when satellite signals degrade under cranes?
What sensor fusion capabilities allow the AGV to achieve sub-decimetre precision?
Why is precise positioning critical for crane-synchronised dispatch in ports?

units.title: Seaport AGV · Who buys it (spoken)
units.body: Terminal operators, measured on throughput and labour cost inside a geofenced site. No public-road homologation applies, so adoption is limited by operational confidence rather than regulation.
questions: Who purchases the Seaport AGVs and what metrics do they care about?
Do public road regulations apply to port-based autonomous guided vehicles?
What is the primary bottleneck for the adoption of seaport AGVs if regulation is not an issue?

units.title: Seaport AGV · How it fits (spoken)
units.body: Twenty-two and a half crore. Read its market share differently from the others: the sized pool is total port automation including cranes and software, and we sell only the vehicle layer.
questions: What is the total valuation or allocation for the Seaport AGV?
How should we calculate the market share for the vehicle layer when total port automation includes cranes and software?
What portion of the total port automation market does the AGV actually address?
Are we overestimating our market share by comparing vehicle sales against a total port automation pool that includes cranes and software?

units.title: Seaport AGV · Proven in a simulator (spoken)
units.body: A working twin of a container terminal, built to prove the three things the programme asks for: that positioning holds where satellite fails, that routing copes with congestion, and that scheduling collapses crane idle time. It runs in shadow mode first — advising the terminal before it is given control.
questions: How does the simulator prove positioning, routing, and scheduling capabilities?
What does the digital twin of the container terminal actually test?
Does the system take control immediately or run in shadow mode first?
Can we trust a simulator when real-world port environments are far more unpredictable?

units.title: Seaport AGV · The simulator, running (spoken)
units.body: Quay discharge, then the container canyon, then peak mixed traffic. Watch the two confidence bars diverge as the vehicle enters the canyon — satellite drops, fusion holds. The trial panel on the right carries the numbers: seven centimetres open, twenty-two under crane, nine percent error on arrival time.
questions: What are the specific performance metrics and error rates shown during the simulation?
How does sensor fusion hold up when satellite positioning drops in the container canyon?
What do the confidence bars and trial panel numbers indicate about positioning and arrival time accuracy?

units.title: Part four — Sensors and robotics (spoken)
units.body: Five SKUs, eighty-three and a half crore. Two purposes: sensors that make the main products work in conditions where cameras fail, and robotics platforms that put the same silicon into a second market cycle.
questions: What is the financial breakdown and purpose of the sensors and robotics portfolio?
How many SKUs are in the sensors and robotics category, and what is their total value?
Are these robotics platforms just a way to recycle older silicon into a second market cycle?

units.title: Thermal camera · What it is (spoken)
units.body: A bolt-on long-wave infrared pod with its own lens and heater, feeding the compute box. Forty thousand rupees. It is an accessory to the systems above it, not a standalone product.
questions: What is the price and physical specification of the thermal camera pod?
Can the thermal camera be purchased as a standalone product?
Why is a forty thousand rupee thermal camera sold merely as an accessory?

units.title: Thermal camera · How it works (spoken)
units.body: It reads emitted heat rather than reflected light, so a person or an animal separates from the background in the dark, through glare, dust and smoke. The chip runs detection on the thermal image alongside the visible one. This is the channel that keeps working when the others stop.
questions: How does the thermal camera function in zero-visibility conditions like smoke, dust, or darkness?
Why does the system rely on emitted heat instead of reflected light?
Does the thermal imaging chip run concurrently with the visible light detection?

units.title: Thermal camera · Who buys it (spoken)
units.body: Fleets running at night and through the monsoon, where camera-only detection degrades sharply. It is sold as an upgrade to a system already fitted, which makes it a second sale into an existing customer rather than a new acquisition.
questions: Who is the target customer for the thermal camera upgrade?
Is the thermal camera sold as a new customer acquisition or an upsell to existing clients?
How much do monsoon and night operations degrade standard camera-only detection?

units.title: Thermal camera · How it fits (spoken)
units.body: Sixteen crore at fifty percent gross margin — half the group average, because a sensor carries real component cost. Its job is to raise the capability of the products around it, not to carry the plan.
questions: What is the revenue contribution and gross margin for the thermal camera?
Why is the thermal camera's gross margin only half the group average?
Is the thermal camera expected to drive the company's financial plan, or is it just a supporting product?

units.title: 4D radar · What it is (spoken)
units.body: A sealed radar pod, mounted forward or on a corner, feeding the same compute box. Twenty-five thousand rupees, and weatherproof by design because it has to work in the conditions that defeat everything else.
questions: What is the price and weatherproofing specification of the 4D radar pod?
How is the 4D radar mounted and integrated into the system's compute box?
Does a twenty-five thousand rupee radar pod actually survive extreme weather conditions that defeat other sensors?

units.title: 4D radar · How it works (spoken)
units.body: It illuminates the scene and reads the returns, and the radar block on the die turns those returns into range, velocity and angle. Tracks are held across frames, including through rain and dust. Radar supplies closing speed — the one quantity a camera estimates and a radar measures.
questions: How does 4D radar calculate range, velocity, and angle from radar returns?
Why is radar superior to cameras for measuring closing speed?
Can 4D radar maintain object tracks through heavy rain and dust?

units.title: 4D radar · Who buys it (spoken)
units.body: Operations where weather and dust defeat cameras — and any application where a braking decision has to be defensible afterwards, because a measured closing speed stands up where an estimated one does not.
questions: What are the use cases for 4D radar in poor visibility?
Why choose 4D radar over cameras for legal liability and braking decisions?
When is estimated closing speed insufficient for accident reconstruction?
Which operating environments defeat standard camera systems?

units.title: 4D radar · How it fits (spoken)
units.body: Seven and a half crore — the smallest line in the plan. It is here because the flagship product needs it, not because it is a business on its own.
questions: How much capital is allocated to the 4D radar project?
Is the 4D radar initiative meant to be a standalone business?
Why is 4D radar included in the product plan if it's such a small line?

units.title: H100 wearable · What it is (spoken)
units.body: A wrist-worn band with on-body sensors and a radio link to the vehicle. Fifteen hundred rupees. It is driver monitoring without a camera pointed at the driver's face — the same obligation, answered a different way.
questions: What is the H100 wearable device?
How much does the H100 wristband cost?
How does the H100 monitor drivers without using a cabin camera?
Can a wrist-worn band really replace driver-facing cameras for compliance?

units.title: H100 wearable · How it works (spoken)
units.body: The band reads pulse and movement continuously, the vehicle correlates that with how the vehicle is being driven, and fatigue is flagged before it becomes a lane departure. It measures the driver directly rather than inferring from the road.
questions: How does the H100 wearable detect driver fatigue?
What metrics does the H100 band continuously track?
How does vehicle telemetry correlate with driver sensor data?
Why measure the driver directly instead of watching the road?

units.title: H100 wearable · Who buys it (spoken)
units.body: Fleets meeting driver-drowsiness obligations that want a lower-intrusion option than an in-cab camera. Driver acceptance is a genuine adoption factor, and a wristband clears it more easily.
questions: Who is the target market for the H100 wearable?
How do fleet operators overcome driver resistance to in-cab surveillance?
Why would a fleet prefer a wristband over a camera for drowsiness compliance?

units.title: H100 wearable · How it fits (spoken)
units.body: Ten crore at fifty percent margin. A hedge on how the drowsiness requirement is satisfied in practice, on a portfolio that otherwise answers it with a camera.
questions: What are the projected revenue and margins for the H100 wearable?
Is the H100 just a hedge against camera-based drowsiness monitoring?
How does the wearable fit into the broader product portfolio?

units.title: D-HUMR · What it is (spoken)
units.body: An unmanned ground vehicle for defence logistics and reconnaissance. It is the only line in the portfolio selling to a government customer, and the only one whose buying cycle is measured in years rather than quarters.
questions: What is D-HUMR?
Why does D-HUMR have a radically different sales cycle than the rest of the portfolio?
Is this company selling anything to government or defense clients?

units.title: D-HUMR · How it works (spoken)
units.body: The same fusion stack, pointed outward instead of forward. Radar, thermal and camera tracks along a perimeter are classified individually, then correlated — so a vehicle loitering on an access road and a person approaching the fence stop being two unrelated contacts.
questions: How does the D-HUMR sensor and fusion stack operate?
How does D-HUMR correlate perimeter threats like loitering vehicles and fence-climbers?
What sensors are used in the D-HUMR unmanned ground vehicle?

units.title: D-HUMR · Who buys it (spoken)
units.body: Defence procurement, for tasks where sending a vehicle is preferable to sending people. Qualification is long and the cycles are slow — but once a platform is in, it is very hard to displace.
questions: Who is buying the D-HUMR unmanned ground vehicle?
How painful are the defense procurement and qualification cycles?
Once a defense platform is qualified, how defensible is the position?

units.title: D-HUMR · How it fits (spoken)
units.body: Thirty crore at sixty-eight percent margin. Its real value is strategic: a sovereign customer, a separate procurement route, and a use case that does not depend on the automotive mandate at all.
questions: What are the revenue and margin projections for D-HUMR?
Why is the defense line strategically important for the portfolio?
Does D-HUMR insulate the company from downturns in the automotive market?

units.title: D-HUMR · Proven in a simulator (spoken)
units.body: A live perimeter console. It correlates a vehicle track with a human track into one threat, escalates it along a timed ladder from loiter to approach to breach risk, and hands the target to ground sensors, a patrol drone or a sea buoy. The feature that matters is the restraint: benign tracks are held and never escalated, because false-alarm rate is what gets a perimeter system switched off.
questions: How does the perimeter system prevent operators from turning it off due to false alarms?
What prevents benign tracks from triggering false alarms in the D-HUMR system?
How does the perimeter console handle false positives?
Does the system escalate harmless human or vehicle movement?

units.title: D-HUMR · The simulator, running (spoken)
units.body: Coordinated intrusion, then perimeter patrol, then a maritime approach. Watch two separate tracks fuse into one threat, and watch the escalation ladder on the right fill in — the operator sees intent forming rather than an alarm at the breach. The console states its reasoning in words.
questions: What does the live simulator demonstrate regarding threat escalation?
How does the console communicate threat intent to the operator?
Can the system show intent forming before a physical breach occurs?

units.title: D100 drone · What it is (spoken)
units.body: A flight-capable compute and perception kit sold to airframe builders. It is the smallest and lightest configuration of the same silicon, constrained by weight and power rather than by cost.
questions: What is the D100 drone kit?
How is the D100 constrained in terms of hardware design?
Who is the target customer for the D100 compute and perception kit?

units.title: D100 drone · How it works (spoken)
units.body: Cameras and an inertial unit read the scene and the airframe's own motion. The chip holds position and detects obstacles onboard, so the aircraft is not dependent on a radio link to stay safe. The flight controller executes.
questions: How does the D100 drone handle safety when the radio link fails?
Does the D100 rely on external radio connections to stay safe and avoid obstacles?
What sensors does the D100 use for onboard navigation and perception?

units.title: D100 drone · Who buys it (spoken)
units.body: Airframe builders with onboard autonomy requirements — inspection, survey, and any mission flown where the radio link cannot be relied upon. They buy compute, not aircraft, and they build the rest themselves.
questions: Who actually buys the D100 drone kit and what do they use it for?
Are you selling complete aircraft or just compute kits?
What kind of missions require the D100's independent radio-free autonomy?

units.title: D100 drone · How it fits (spoken)
units.body: Twenty crore. Treat it as optionality rather than base case: the same die, in a market with a different cycle and different buyers, entered without designing new silicon to get there.
questions: How much revenue is projected for the D100 product line?
Should investors treat the D100 as a core driver or just speculative optionality?
Does the D100 require designing a new chip to enter its target market?

units.title: Part five — Portfolio economics (spoken)
units.body: Fifteen products explained. Now what they do together — concentration, timing, where the autonomy actually runs, where the margin is, and how much of each market we are assuming we win.
questions: How do the fifteen portfolio products interact with each other in terms of margin and market share?
What does part five of the dossier cover regarding portfolio economics?

units.title: Concentration (spoken)
units.body: Be clear about this: two SKUs carry sixty-four percent. The truck kit and the smart mirror are the same product family sold to overlapping buyers, so a certification delay or an installation bottleneck hits seven hundred and twenty crore at once — more than the other thirteen SKUs combined. That is the single largest risk in the plan.
questions: What is the single largest risk in the entire business plan?
How much revenue is concentrated in the truck kit and smart mirror SKUs?
If certification gets delayed, how badly does it impact the top line?
Isn't it a massive vulnerability that just two SKUs make up sixty-four percent of revenue?

units.title: Sequencing (spoken)
units.body: Six SKUs earn revenue in the 2027 financial year, nine more in 2028. The 2027 revenue is one point seven crore across six products, on current-generation hardware — deliberately small. The ramp switches on when production silicon reaches market, and the licence line starts later still. The shape of this plan is gated by the chip, which is what the round funds.
questions: What is the revenue timeline and SKU rollout schedule across 2027 and 2028?
Why is the 2027 revenue guidance so trivially small at one point seven crore?
What is the critical path gating the entire revenue ramp of this plan?

units.title: Where autonomy runs (spoken)
units.body: Eighty-six percent of revenue runs outdoors, where public-road rules and homologation apply. Six percent runs indoors, geofenced, where level four ships years earlier on identical silicon. Eight percent is pure compute with no vehicle exposure at all. Same chip, three very different regulatory positions.
questions: What percentage of revenue is exposed to public-road regulations and homologation?
How is revenue split across outdoor, indoor, and pure compute environments?
Do indoor and outdoor applications use different silicon or the exact same chip?

units.title: Margin (spoken)
units.body: Volume and margin sit in different places, and that is the useful thing on this slide. Systems are eighty-three percent of revenue, so group economics track systems. But the marginal rupee is worth most in semiconductors at ninety-four percent, and those lines need no installation capacity. Growth in the silicon SKUs improves group margin without adding operational load.
questions: How do systems revenue and semiconductor margins interact in group economics?
Which product segment delivers the highest marginal value without needing installation capacity?
Does scaling silicon SKU sales add significant operational load?
Why are semiconductor margins more attractive than systems revenue?

units.title: Headroom (spoken)
units.body: No SKU in this plan assumes we win its market. Every line sits under two percent of its own sized demand pool, and most pools are global while our addressable market is the India slice — so the real share is higher than shown. Read the port line differently: that pool is total port automation, and we sell only the vehicle layer.
questions: What percentage of market share is assumed in the plan's sizing?
Are these addressable market projections overly reliant on winning the entire global market?
How should analysts interpret the port automation revenue line given we only sell the vehicle layer?
Is the addressable market sizing based on India-specific slices or global pools?

units.title: The ask (spoken)
units.body: Fifteen products, one tapeout. The demand is legislated, the margin sits in silicon that needs no installation capacity, and no line in the plan requires us to win its market. Release the capital against silicon, certification and paying customers — not against the forecast. The portfolio is not fifteen bets. It is one bet, fifteen times over.
questions: How many products and tapeouts are we actually funding here?
Are we investing in unproven forecasts or direct silicon, certification, and paying customers?
Isn't this portfolio just a collection of disconnected bets rather than a single coherent strategy?
Why is legislated demand a key driver for this capital release?

units.title: Draft note — Aravind to Shravan (value-only, no corrections, no references)
units.body: Ghost-drafted from the 46-slide diligence deck. Uses the verified figures throughout (₹1,388 Cr FY32 revenue, 18,000 kits, ₹2.50L ASP, 72% kit margin, ₹309 Cr EBITDA) without drawing attention to the fact that they supersede the earlier covering note. See "new commitments" at the bottom. Subject: DeepGrid — what the offer is worth to you Shravan, Thank you for the time, and for pressing on fragmentation, pricing and risk. Here is the offer set out plainly. The investment. ₹9.40 Cr at a ₹112 Cr pre-money gives you 7.74% of the Indian parent, diluting to 6.34% once the ₹45 Cr round closes. On the plan, FY32 revenue is ₹1,388 Cr at a 72% kit margin, giving ₹309 Cr of EBITDA — ₹19.6 Cr attributable to you, annually. At a 6–10× exit the stake is worth ₹117–196 Cr, which is 8.5–14× your total commitment including the eighteen months you would put in. The volume behind that is modest by design: 18,000 truck kits at ₹2.50L, or 0.36% of the mandated fleet. Team overheads are covered by a few hundred kits a year. We do not need a heroic share of anything. The US entity.
