units.title: Top Global Commercial Vehicle OEM Chooses Aptiv’s Gen 6 ADAS Platform
units.body: Press Release January 06, 2026 Scalable, turn-key solution tailored for India’s traffic and road conditions, delivers safe navigation and cost-effective regulatory compliance. Integrates Aptiv’s latest radar and smart camera—featuring STRADVISION’s AI-based vision technology—with Aptiv’s modular software solutions, all optimized for commercial vehicle applications. SCHAFFHAUSEN, Switzerland — Aptiv PLC (NYSE: APTV), a global industrial technology company, today announced that a leading commercial vehicle OEM (Original Equipment Manufacturer) has selected its Gen 6 Advanced Driver Assistance System (ADAS) to equip its future trucks and buses in India. This agreement marks Aptiv’s first collaboration with an Indian commercial vehicle OEM on ADAS. It comes as the industry prepares for 2027 regulations requiring new trucks and buses to include safety features such as automatic emergency braking, lane departure and blind spot warnings and pedestrian and obstacle detection when starting from a stop. To meet these requirements, commercial vehicle OEMs face unique challenges. They must integrate advanced safety technologies across diverse vehicle types and powertrains, address larger blind spots, and ensure reliability in harsh environments. units.title: Verdict
units.body: The arithmetic is clean. Every stated capture % reproduces exactly from its own formula, and the revenue build ties to the P&L to the rupee (₹1,128.45 Cr FY32, 15 lines). The problem is not the numbers — it is that one column silently mixes two incompatible denominators, and the product the whole story rests on is the one using the flattering basis. The tab's own closing claim — "our FY32 volumes are a single-digit share of each pool" — is false for AD2 on the sheet's own dominant methodology and its own stated TAM.

units.title: Finding 1 — "Capture %" is two different metrics in one column
units.body: Basis Products Formula shape Revenue ÷ revenue AD0, Seaport AGV, A100, Chipset, Thermal, 4D radar (6) ='Revenue Build'!J61 10000000/Assumptions!$C$6/1e9/3.09 Units ÷ units AD2, Autonomous TaaS (2) =C22/1000000 None given AD1, H100, D-HUMR, D100 (4) — Six rows convert ₹Cr → USD at ₹94/$ and divide by a dollar market. Two divide unit counts by unit counts. They sit under one header, in one column, and are summarised in one sentence. They are not comparable, and the column gives the reader no way to know.

units.title: Finding 2 — On its own revenue basis, AD2 is 23.9%, not 1.8%
units.body: AD2 is the mandate story: 18,000 units, ₹450 Cr, 40% of FY32 revenue. - As shown: 18,000 ÷ 1,000,000 units = 1.8% - On the sheet's dominant basis: ₹450 Cr = $47.9M against the sheet's own row 8, "TAM — mandated ADAS (AIS-184/186/187/188) annual = $200M" → 23.9% Both use the sheet's own numbers. A 13x swing rests on a choice the sheet never states. 23.9% of a regulated market by FY32 is a defensible plan — but it is a different plan from the one "1.8%" describes, and it invites a different diligence question.

units.title: Finding 3 — The 1.0M SAM adds a flow to a stock
units.body: Row 9 builds SAM as ~500k new/yr + ~500k retrofit. The first is an annual flow; the second is a one-time stock of existing N2/N3 vehicles, mandated from Oct 2026. By FY32 — five years into the retrofit window — that stock is substantially converted, so it should not still sit in an FY32 denominator at full value. On the annual flow alone, AD2 capture is 3.6%.

units.title: Finding 4 — Two sheets disagree on whether AD0 is mandate-driven
units.body: AD0 is 54,000 units and ₹270 Cr — 24% of FY32 revenue, the second-largest line. - Revenue Build J44 labels it: "AD0 Smart Mirror (mandate retrofit)" - Demand & TAM row 17 says: "NOT mandated — voluntary safety/convenience buy" Mandate-driven and voluntary demand carry different risk, different sales cycles, and different defensibility. One of these is wrong, and a quarter of FY32 revenue turns on which.

units.title: What to change before this goes in front of an investor
units.body: 1. Split the column in two — Capture % (revenue) and Capture % (units) — or convert everything to revenue ÷ revenue. Do not leave one header over two metrics. 2. Show AD2 on the revenue basis and defend 23.9%. The mandate is the strongest thing in this plan. A sophisticated reader will recompute it, find 23.9%, and wonder why 1.8% was the number on the page. Leading with 23.9% and the mandate floor is the stronger position. 3. Split SAM into flow and stock with a retrofit-conversion curve, so the FY32 denominator is an FY32 denominator. 4. Resolve the AD0 mandate question and make both sheets say the same thing. 5. Size the remaining four, or say plainly they are unsized — and add T100.

units.title: Checks
units.body: Verified - Every stated capture % recomputed independently from its formula and source cells; all 9 tie exactly. - Revenue build FY32 (15 lines) = ₹1,128.45 Cr = P&L row 6 FY2032. Exact. - Unit counts on this tab traced cell-by-cell to Revenue Build J44–J58; all 12 tie. - FX ₹94/$ read from Assumptions!C6, the same cell every revenue-basis formula uses. - AD2 $47.9M and the $200M TAM both taken from this workbook, not from outside sources. Not verified - No external market size was checked. IMARC, EMR, Dataintelo, SNS Insider, Verified MR and the rest are taken as stated. The $200M mandated-ADAS TAM in particular drives Finding 2 and was not independently sourced. - The business-plan workbook was not analysed — this brief covers the financial model only. - Retrofit-conversion timing in Finding 3 is a stated assumption; the sheet carries no curve to test. - The regulatory claims (GSR 184(E) dates, the AEBS deferral to Oct 2027) were not checked. units.title: BLUF
units.body: Four findings change the deck. Two correct errors I introduced, one strengthens the case, one weakens a stated strength. 1. The deck flags a mandate-date conflict that does not exist. Slide 27 says the verification "carries two different 2027 dates — pin the exact instrument and date." The gazette resolves it: 1 January 2027 (new models) and 1 October 2027 (all models) are one two-stage timetable under rule 96(12), not a contradiction. Ask #8 and next-step #10 should be deleted, and the instrument named: G.S.R. 834(E), 11 Nov 2025, amending G.S.R. 184(E) which was only ever a draft. 2. The "~20× the compliance anchor" comparison is cross-scope and overstates the gap against DeepGrid's own interest. It sets a ₹2.50L capital purchase against a device sticker price. Against the AIS-140 three-year total cost of ownership — ₹22,400 basic / ₹40,600 standard / ₹62,200 enterprise — the like-for-like ratio is 4.0×–11.2×, not ~20×. The pricing contest is materially less lopsided than the deck says, and the correction favours the company. 3. "2.8–6.5× cheaper than imports" cannot be verified and should be demoted. No public per-unit India price exists for Mobileye EyeQ6, Bosch/Continental, Qualcomm SA8295 or Nvidia Orin. bitsensing — the one comparable product with a live India launch —

units.title: The one thing that survives untouched, and it matters
units.body: No vendor in the cohort holds Indian ADAS certification — and AIS-162 itself is still listed as "Draft" on the MoRTH AIS register. The deck's central competitive claim — "the window is the asset here, not the price gap" — is the claim that survived this run best. It is also the claim that does not depend on any price. That is the argument to lead with. The price gap is unverifiable; the certification window is real and documented.

units.title: What the pricing evidence actually implies for the commercial thesis
units.body: The AIS-140 precedent is the closest domestic analogue and it points somewhere specific: over three years, the platform licence can exceed hardware cost by 2–3×. Value in that market went to whoever held the recurring compliance relationship, not to whoever sold the box. Combined with the ~8-year notification-to-enforcement lag on AIS-140, this supports two things the deck already argues and one it does not: - supports the transitional-enforcement reading (slide 6) - supports "price the function, not the bundle" (slide 30) - not yet in the deck: it argues for AD3 (the rented kit) being the strategically right commercial model rather than the pricing anomaly slide 31 currently calls it. The ₹0.66 Cr/yr figure still does not reconcile at ~26× the outright sale — but the direction (recurring over capital) is what the domestic precedent rewards.

units.title: Contested, not resolved: the FY32 margin basis
units.body: A prior run derived 77.2% as the honest blended FY32 gross margin at a 72% kit margin. Reproducing it here: 77.2% blended requires 87.2% gross margin on the ₹474.30 Cr of non-ADAS revenue. That is not more defensible than the deck's flat 72% — it simply moves the assumption from "non-ADAS earns what the kit earns" to "non-ADAS earns 87.2%", and neither is disclosed anywhere in BP-1A. Recommendation: show the range, not a point. FY32 EBITDA is ₹309 Cr to ₹381 Cr depending on non-ADAS margin (72% → 87.2%), with attributable earnings of ₹19.6 Cr to ₹24.2 Cr. Both ends still sit far below the stated ₹536.63 Cr, so the 120% impossibility finding on slide 15 is unaffected — only the rebuilt figure widens.

units.title: Source bias — stated plainly
units.body: The AIS-140 price evidence (EV-09 … EV-13) comes predominantly from fleetx, a fleet telematics vendor publishing buyer guides. Three of four price rows trace to one commercial publisher with an interest in emphasising total cost of ownership over sticker price. That bias runs in the same direction as the finding it supports — a telematics vendor benefits from readers concluding the box is more expensive than it looks. The finding is therefore directionally suspect and is labelled medium confidence, not high, and the deck should attribute it rather than assert it. Corroboration from a non-telematics source (an RTO circular, an operator association, a fleet's own procurement note) is the single highest-value next retrieval.

units.title: Decision: no composite competitor score is issued
units.body: The contract fails a run where "scores or charts use undefined metrics" and where "source coverage is uneven but confidence is hidden". Both conditions would apply to a ranked competitor score here: - 4 of 7 cohort members have unit price = UNVERIFIED (EV-20 … EV-23) - 0 of 7 hold Indian ADAS certification (EV-08 and the deck's own table) - the two strongest India-present competitors found (bitsensing, ZF WABCO) publish no unit price at all (EV-16) A weighted score across those inputs would rank source availability, not competitive position, and would then be charted as if it were the latter. That is precisely the error the ledger exists to prevent.

units.title: A1 — The regulation is cited wrongly, and the deck contradicts itself · CRITICAL
units.body: Slide 4 says naming GSR 184e in client-facing material is "defensible" and that the "gazette notification itself" is outstanding. Slide 12 says "Stop any external claim citing G.S.R.184(E) as final law." Both are in the same delivered deck. Slide 12 is right. G.S.R. 184(E) (20 Mar 2025) was only ever a draft. The notified instrument is G.S.R. 834(E), 11 Nov 2025, amended by G.S.R. 862(E), gazetted 21 Nov 2025 — and its own preamble names 184(E) as the draft it supersedes ( EV-REG-02 ). The gazette is not outstanding; it has been public for nine months. The strings "834" and "862" appear nowhere in the 83 slides. Root cause: Round 2's live research took ZF's press note and Aptiv's release — both of which repeat "GSR 184e" ( EV-ZF-05 ) — as corroboration of the instrument. Vendors repeating a draft is not evidence of law. A prior run had already read the gazette text; that finding was overwritten by a weaker source. Fix: rewrite slide 4's regulatory row; add the instrument, both rule references and the two-stage timetable; keep slide 12's stop-rule and make it consistent.

units.title: A2 — Starkenn's headline number cannot be stated · HIGH
units.body: "2,500+ vehicles" appears on slides 19, 20 and 83 — including the hostile-question slide ("Starkenn shows 2,500+ vehicles. Are we not already behind?"). The single source behind it (YourStory, Nov 2024) contains three mutually inconsistent figures in one interview: "over 2,500 vehicles", "over 700 units sold", and "300+ vehicles have deployed our tech" ( EV-STK-04 ). The dossier propagated the largest. It is self-reported, un-audited and ~21 months old. Compounding it: Starkenn is a 57-person company, shrinking 15.8% YoY, with $2.0m of lifetime funding ( EV-STK-05 ) — none of which is in the deck. Fix: remove the number. Argue Starkenn from its 30% government-tender share and subscription model, which is the durable point, and answer the hostile question with the source contradiction rather than conceding it.

units.title: B3 — No distinction between systems that brake and systems that warn · CRITICAL
units.body: The dossier runs one heatmap across all competitors. But the market divides at brake actuation: - Reach actuation (AEBS): ZF, Aptiv+STRADVISION — can satisfy rule 96(12) - Warning-only: drivebuddyAI (camera-only, alerts driver), bitsensing (explicitly no AEB), Starkenn — cannot satisfy rule 96(12) at any price These are two different markets, two different buyers and two different clocks. The warning-only group is winning retrofit fleet-safety budget today; the actuating group is competing for homologation budget in 2027. Flattening them makes drivebuddyAI look like a mandate competitor when it is not, and makes the mandate look nearer than it is.

units.title: B4 — No certification-gate view
units.body: ISO 26262, ARAI certification and AEC-Q100 are the actual gates, and no slide compares who holds what. STRADVISION holds ISO 26262 ( EV-SV-05 ); ZF claims ARAI certification without publishing certificate numbers ( EV-ZF-04 ); Gahan's AEC-Q100 claim is a category error ( EV-GHN-05 ); Netrasemi has none; DeepGrid has no published pathway. This is the real barrier, and it is nowhere as a single exhibit.

units.body: Aptiv ships over-the-air updates via LINC + VxWorks ( EV-APT-06 ). That turns ADAS from a shipped part into a maintained service and keeps the customer relationship with the integrator. A merchant module vendor has no answer to it. Not mentioned anywhere.

units.title: The preamble is decisive on G.S.R. 184(E)
units.body: The notified rule states it was made "following consideration of public objections and suggestions to draft rules published as G.S.R 184(E) dated 20th March, 2025, under section 212(1) of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988." G.S.R. 184(E) is therefore named, by the operative instrument itself, as the superseded draft. It is not the law and cannot be cited as the compliance hook.

units.title: What G.S.R. 862(E) changed
units.body: It substituted rule 96(12) to read "Vehicle Stability Function as per IS 11852:2019 and Advanced Emergency Braking Systems, as per AIS-162". The operative AEBS provision is 862(E)'s text, not 834(E)'s. Any citation of 834(E) alone for AEBS is incomplete. Also substituted rule 93(1)(B)(i) so ADAS sensors and casings (BSIS, MOIS) are excluded from overall-width measurement.
questions: How did G.S.R. 862(E) change the requirements for AEBS?
Are ADAS sensors included in the legal measurement of a vehicle's width?
Which specific rule governs the exclusion of sensor casings from width limits?

units.title: Precision note on secondary reporting
units.body: Fortune India (13 Feb 2026) reports IS 11852:2019 and "ESC under AIS 162" as mandatory "from October 1, 2027", dropping the 1 Jan 2027 new-model stage and naming ESC where the instrument says Vehicle Stability Function. Secondary trade press garbles this timetable in both directions — use the gazette text.
questions: Is the trade press reporting accurate dates for ADAS implementation?
Does the mandate require 'ESC' or 'Vehicle Stability Function'?
Which secondary sources are misreporting the January 2027 deadline?

units.title: Source manifest — DeepGrid Semi Pre-Series A IM review
units.body: One source set = one job. Every row gets a stable ID; every claim in every output cites one. A source that is not in this table cannot be cited, and a claim that cites nothing does not ship. - Job: DeepGrid Semi Pre-Series A IM review - Decision this must serve: Decide whether IM v2 is investor-ready, or what must be fixed before it goes out - Opened: 2026-08-15 ID Title Type Origin Retrieved Trust S1 DeepGrid Semi - IM - v2.pdf pdf sources/DeepGrid Semi - IM - v2.pdf 2026-08-15 unrated S2 EXA-FINDINGS-DECK-CONTRADICTIONS.md md runs/2026-08-10-deepgrid-gtm-icp-playbook/ (repo) 2026-08-10 secondary S3 RECONCILIATION.md md runs/2026-08-10-deepgrid-gtm-icp-playbook/ (repo) 2026-08-10 secondary S4 GBrain: DeepGrid — India ADAS mandate and competitive evidence gbrain slug deepgrid-india-adas-mandate-and-competitive-evidence-2026-08 2026-08-08 secondary S5 GBrain: DeepGrid Semi — client acquisition findings gbrain slug deepgrid-semi-client-acquisition-2026-08 2026-08-05 secondary S6 GBrain: DeepGrid India ADAS competitor landscape gbrain slug deepgrid-india-adas-competitor-landscape-2026-08-13 2026-08-13 secondary S7 GBrain: DeepGrid GTM & ICP playbook deck gbrain slug deepgrid-gtm-icp-playbook-deck-2026-08 2026-08-10 secondary S8 Govt mandates advanced safety technologies for heavy CV
questions: What sources were used to audit the DeepGrid Semi investment memo?
Is every claim in the review properly tied to an identifiable source ID?

units.title: Stage 1 Audit — DeepGrid Semi Pre-Series A IM v2
units.body: Objective: decide whether IM v2 is investor-ready, or what must be fixed first. Source: DeepGrid Semi — IM — v2.pdf, June 2026, 27 pages, Emani Capital Advisory. Scope limit: single-source audit. This finds internal contradictions only. Nothing here is checked against the outside world — that is Stage 2's job, and it is not done. No recommendation is given in this stage, by design.
questions: What is the scope and limitation of the Stage 1 audit on the DeepGrid IM?
Does this initial audit check the company's claims against the real world?

units.title: 1. What we know with reasonable confidence
units.body: These are internally consistent and arithmetically check out. - The raise is USD $4.0–5.0M, pre-Series A, equity / compulsorily convertible. - The FY2032 revenue build is coherent across all three cross-tabs on p.21. Business line, product category, and revenue type each independently sum to the same total: 75.0 + 33.5 + 1229.5 + 50.0, and 75.0 + 33.5 + 153.0 + 966.2 + 110.3 + 50.0, and 75.0 + 1197.0 + 66.0 + 50.0. All three land on 1,388.0. - The P&L on p.20 is self-consistent: gross profit 1226.5 on revenue 1388.0 is the stated 88% GM; EBITDA 536.6 on 1388.0 is 38.7%. - The TOPS derivation is correct: 64 PCOREs x 512 MACs = 32,768 MACs; x 600 MHz x 2 ops = 39.3 TOPS INT8. Stated on p.8 and reproduced on p.15. - The MicroDC-A1 spec block is internally coherent: 4 chips x 4.19 PF = 16.76 PFLOPS; 4 x 280 W = 1,120 W; 1,024 tiles x 4 = 4,096. - FY2027 revenue of 6.0 Cr reconciles between the P&L and the business-line table. - Traction claims are specific and dated: 15 provisional patents filed Mar 2026 (IN2026/DGR/001-015), 1 Cr defence revenue received Q1 2026 on FPGA hardware, YOLOv11n at 40fps measured on Artix-7 200T.
questions: Which parts of the financial model and technical specs actually check out?
Are the revenue projections and P&L arithmetic internally consistent in the IM?
What is the basis for the stated TOPS and chip specifications?

units.title: 2. What is being assumed
units.body: Assumptions presented in the document's own voice, with what would confirm each. - The mandate converts to purchases. GSR 184(E) is described as "a regulatory floor, not a forecast". Enforcement existing is not the same as fleets buying on schedule. Confirmed by: signed fleet orders, not the gazette notification. - ASIC economics arrive as modelled. Gross margin goes 53% - 88% between FY2027 and FY2032, resting on the FPGA-to-ASIC transition. Confirmed by: first silicon returning to spec, which the timeline places at Q4 2026. - Sales and marketing at 12–14% of revenue holds while revenue compounds from 6.0 Cr to 1,388.0 Cr — a 231x increase over five years on a roughly flat S&M ratio. Confirmed by: cost-per-design-win from the first fleet cohort. - "No indigenous alternative exists". Confirmed by: an independent scan, not by the company's own competitive slide. - The India-data moat compounds. Stated as structural. Confirmed by: a measured accuracy delta on Indian road data versus a foreign stack — a number the IM does not have.
questions: What major operational and commercial assumptions are we blindly trusting in this thesis?
Is regulatory enforcement enough to guarantee that fleets will actually buy on schedule?
Does the company have any proof that their gross margin leap and sales efficiency targets are realistic?

units.title: 3.1 The headline revenue number is wrong, and it is on the cover — CRITICAL
units.body: Location Figure p.3 cover stat " ₹1,128 Cr — Revenue FY2032E" p.21 slide title "Revenue to ₹1,128 Crore by FY2032" p.5 platform cascade " ₹1,388 Cr by FY32" p.6 investment thesis "Total group revenue: ₹1,388 Cr FY32" p.20 P&L, FY2032 row " 1388.0 " p.21's own table, directly beneath its title sums to 1,388.0 A ₹260 Cr gap, 23% of the number. It appears on the cover — the most-read figure in the document — and again as a slide title contradicting the table printed under it. The ₹1,388 Cr figure is the supported one: three independent cross-tabs and the P&L agree.
questions: Why does the cover of the pitch deck show a completely different revenue number than the financial tables inside?
How did a massive 260 Crore error make it onto the cover of the investment memo?
Which revenue figure is the correct one, given the conflicting numbers in the document?

units.title: 3.3 SAM exceeds TAM — structurally impossible
units.body: p.7: " ₹61,000 Cr India ADAS aftermarket TAM by 2030". p.14: "India SAM (5M+ trucks mandated) ₹85,000 Cr ". A serviceable available market cannot exceed the total addressable market it sits inside. p.14 also lists a "Retrofit market (9Cr vehicles) ₹4,50,000 Cr", which makes the ₹61,000 Cr TAM smaller than two other markets on the same page. Either the TAM is scoped far more narrowly than its label says, or the figures come from different definitions that were never reconciled.
questions: How incompetent is the market sizing when the Serviceable Addressable Market is larger than the Total Addressable Market?
Where did these contradictory market size figures on page 14 come from?

units.title: 3.4 Die cost stated three different ways — on a slide about not confusing costs
units.body: Location Die cost p.4 "the die is ~$30, not $6,000" p.8 " <$3 die · ~$30 board BOM" p.22 headline " <$4 Die Cost (at 1M chips)" p.22 body, same box "Die ( $3 ) + carrier board + connectors + packaging = ~$30" p.4 has mistaken the board BOM for the die. p.22 is titled "Cost Clarity — Three Numbers VCs Always Confuse" and contradicts itself between its own headline and body. This is the most quotable failure in the document, because the slide's entire purpose is precision about this number.
questions: How can a slide titled Cost Clarity manage to contradict its own die cost numbers?
Did the founders really confuse the board BOM with the die cost on the very slide warning VCs not to confuse them?

units.title: 3.5 NRE / tapeout cost: five figures, never reconciled
units.body: $630K MPW shuttle (p.15, p.16) · $2M "we spend" (p.22) · $2.42M NRE (p.8, p.15) · ~$3M NRE headline (p.22) · $3.17M tapeout (p.5). Some of these are legitimately different things — an MPW shuttle is not full production NRE. The document never says which is which, and p.22 puts "~$3M" and "we spend $2M" in the same box.
questions: Why are there multiple conflicting figures for NRE and tapeout costs in the dossier?
Does the document distinguish between an MPW shuttle and full production NRE?
Why does the dossier lump different chip fabrication expenses together under roughly three million dollars?

units.title: 3.6 Die area: 57.1mm² vs 42mm²
units.body: p.8, p.15 and p.6 all state ~ 57.1mm². p.16 states "68.7 effective TOPS on a 42mm² die". These are reconcilable — the six chiplet areas on p.15 (7+6+7+8+7+7) sum to exactly 42mm², so 42 is silicon area and 57.1 is the combo die. The document never says so, and p.16 calls 42mm² "a die". p.16 also introduces "68.7 effective TOPS" against 39.3 TOPS peak everywhere else, with no definition of "effective".
questions: How is the die area discrepancy between 57.1 square millimeters and 42 square millimeters reconciled?
What does effective TOPS mean when it contradicts the peak TOPS figure everywhere else?
Why does the documentation fail to define effective compute performance clearly?

units.title: 3.8 AD2 sensor count: 6 cameras, 9 cameras, or 6+LiDAR+ultrasonic
units.body: p.8 title: " 6 Cameras. One Chip." · p.9: " 9 CAM + 2 RADAR FUSED", itemising 7x RGB + 2 thermal + 2 radar = 11 channels, no LiDAR, no ultrasonic · p.13 pricing: AD2 = " 6 Cam + 2 Radar + LiDAR + 4 US " · p.15: A100 is " 6-camera MIPI CSI-2". Three different sensor configurations for the same AD2 product. The p.13 spec includes LiDAR and 4 ultrasonic sensors that the p.9 architecture diagram does not carry, which also puts the ₹2–2.5L kit BOM in question.
questions: How many cameras and sensors are actually included in the AD2 product architecture?
Why do the sensor counts differ across the architecture diagram, the pricing page, and the camera specs?
Does the kit bill of materials actually include LiDAR and ultrasonic sensors despite being omitted from the main diagrams?

units.title: 3.10 The "3 to 7x cheaper" claim does not match its own table
units.body: p.14 claims " 3 to 7x Cheaper Than Every Import" and lists imports at ₹5–8L (Mobileye), ₹8–12L (Continental), ₹12–18L (Nvidia), ₹10–15L (Qualcomm) against DGrid at ₹2–2.5L. Worst case against the cheapest import: ₹5L / ₹2.5L = 2.0x, below the claimed floor of 3x. Best case against the dearest: ₹18L / ₹2L = 9.0x, above the claimed ceiling of 7x. The true range from their own numbers is roughly 2x to 9x. The claim understates the strongest comparison and overstates the weakest. Separately, p.19 prices Mobileye SuperVision at "~₹3.5L" while p.14 puts Mobileye at ₹5–8L. Against ₹3.5L the multiple is 1.4x.
questions: Is the three to seven times cheaper claim supported by the company's own pricing table?
Why does the competitive pricing comparison understate the strongest competitor matchup and overstate the weakest?
How does the claimed price advantage hold up if Mobileye SuperVision is priced much lower than stated in the main comparison?

units.title: 3.11 The 200x utilisation claim strains its own arithmetic
units.body: p.16 states competitors achieve " 1–5% hardware utilisation" and that DGrid's ALU is "active 200x longer per cycle". 200x of 1% is 200%, and of 5% is 1,000% — both impossible. The claim only works if the competitor baseline is at or below 0.5%, which is outside the range the same paragraph states.
questions: How can hardware utilization be active 200 times longer per cycle when basic math makes that percentage impossible?
What unrealistic baseline assumptions are required to make the 200x utilization claim work?
Why does the deck include performance utilization claims that violate basic arithmetic?

units.title: 4. Conclusions supported by more than one place in the document
units.body: - FY2032 revenue of ₹1,388 Cr — four independent locations (p.5, p.6, p.20 P&L, p.21 tables). - 39.3 TOPS INT8 peak — stated and independently derivable on p.8 and p.15. - 15 provisional patents, filed March 2026, expiring March 2027 — p.3, p.6, p.15, p.18, p.26 all agree. - ₹1 Cr defence revenue received — p.3, p.15, p.18, p.26 agree, and it is described as received rather than contracted. - TSMC 28nm HPC+, ~57.1mm², six chiplets — p.8, p.15 agree.
questions: Which financial and technical metrics are consistent across multiple sections of the dossier?
What is the projected revenue for FY2032 and how many times is it stated in the document?
What are the confirmed details regarding the peak TOPS, provisional patents, and received defence revenue?

units.title: 5. What is missing
units.body: Ranked by how much each would move an investment decision. 1. A cap table, current valuation, and the pre/post-money split. A $4–5M raise document with no ownership terms. p.18 says an IBBI valuation is "in progress" and "expected prior to term-sheet signing" — so the number does not exist yet. 2. Any historical financials. The P&L starts at FY2027 projections. There is no FY2025 or FY2026 actual, no balance sheet, no current cash position, no burn rate, no runway. For a company with ₹1 Cr of received revenue, the audited past is one page and it is absent. 3. Customer evidence behind the 231x revenue ramp. ₹88L MCEME pipeline is named; nothing else is. No LOIs, no named fleet pilots, no design-in commitments from the Tata or Mahindra evaluations the milestones reference. 4. Unit economics at the FY2027–2029 volumes, where FPGA GM is 46.7% on AD2. The 88% GM story is an FY2032 endpoint; the years that consume the raise are the thin-margin ones and they are not broken out per unit. 5. What happens if first silicon fails. 54% of proceeds go to ASIC tapeout NRE. There is no contingency, no second-shuttle budget, and no stated consequence for the revenue model if Q4 2026 silicon does not come back functional. 6. Founder/CTO equity, vesting,
questions: What critical financial information and cap table details are completely missing from this fundraising document?
Where are the historical financials, balance sheets, and burn rate data for this raise?
What customer evidence or signed commitments exist to back up the projected revenue ramp beyond a small pipeline mention?
What are the unit economics and gross margins for the early years before reaching the terminal endpoint?
What contingency plan is in place if first silicon fails, given how much cash goes to tape-out?

units.title: 6. Unanswered questions that could change the decision
units.body: - Is FY2032 revenue ₹1,128 Cr or ₹1,388 Cr — and if the deck cannot hold that number steady, what else moved? - What is the pre-money valuation, and against what evidence? - Is there a signed order beyond the ₹1 Cr defence receipt? - What is current cash and runway to first silicon? - Is the ₹61,000 Cr TAM or the ₹85,000 Cr SAM the real figure, and under whose definition? - Does the ₹2–2.5L AD2 kit price include the LiDAR and 4 ultrasonic sensors p.13 lists? - What is the accuracy delta of the India-trained model versus a foreign stack, measured?
questions: What is the actual FY2032 revenue projection given that the deck fluctuates between conflicting figures?
What is the pre-money valuation and what valuation report backs it up?
Are there any signed customer orders or commercial traction beyond the initial defence receipt?
How much cash does the company have left and what is the runway to first silicon?
What is the accuracy delta of the domestic model compared to foreign alternatives, and has it been measured?

units.title: Limitations
units.body: Single-source audit. Every finding above is the document disagreeing with itself; none of it establishes whether any claim is true. The market sizing, the regulatory reading, the competitor prices, and the technical benchmarks are all unverified against external sources. Stage 2 has not been run.
questions: Are any of the claims in this dossier verified against external market sources?
Is this audit based on a single source, and do external benchmarks support their technical and pricing claims?

units.title: Verification
units.body: - Run 2026-08-15. All 11 contradictions in section 3 were located by reading the source pages directly, then re-derived from the figures printed on those pages rather than from any summary of them. - Arithmetic re-derived independently: the three p.21 cross-tab sums (all 1,388.0), the P&L gross margin (1226.5/1388.0 = 88.4%), the EBITDA margin (536.6/1388.0 = 38.7%), the TOPS derivation (32,768 x 600e6 x 2 / 1e12 = 39.3), the chiplet area sum (42mm²), the MicroDC compute and power totals, and the price-multiple range (2.0x–9.0x). - Gate: check output.py --strict against SOURCES.md. - NOT VERIFIED: no claim was checked against any source outside.
questions: How were the contradictions and arithmetic in the dossier verified?
Were any of the company's claims checked against independent external sources or only internally against itself?

units.title: Stage 2 — Gap ranking and fill — DeepGrid Semi IM v2
units.body: Stage 1 audited the document against itself. This stage checks it against the world. Tool order followed: local repo files first, then GBrain recall, then Exa. Local and GBrain answered most of it — this engagement has seven prior DeepGrid runs and four compiled GBrain pages, and they had already verified the two facts that matter most. Headline: the IM's central "Why Now" is false, and prior work in this repo told them so before this IM was written.
questions: What did prior repo work and previous runs reveal about the central thesis of the IM?
Did the audit check the IM against internal consistency or external reality?

units.title: C1. The mandate the whole thesis rests on is a draft that never became law
units.body: The IM's first reason to invest: "MoRTH GSR 184(E) enforcement is live — April 2026. Every N2/N3 truck sold after this date requires ADAS compliance… Regulatory floor, not a forecast." It repeats April 2026 on p.3, p.6, p.7 and p.26. G.S.R. 184(E) (20 Mar 2025) was only ever a draft notification. The notified rule is G.S.R. 834(E), 11 Nov 2025, in force 12 Nov 2025, amended by G.S.R. 862(E) of 21 Nov 2025. The binding dates are: System Standard New models All models AEBS + stability AIS-162 / IS 11852:2019 1 Jan 2027 1 Oct 2027 LDWS AIS-188 1 Oct 2027 1 Jan 2028 DDAWS / BSIS / MOIS AIS-184/186/187 (rule 125Q) 1 Oct 2027 1 Jan 2028 Independently corroborated outside this repo: Fortune India reports AEBS and stability control mandatory from 1 October 2027, and BSIS/MOIS/DDAWS/LDWS from 1 January 2028, notified vide GSR 834(E) dated 11 November 2025. MoRTH's own AIS register still lists AIS-162 with status "Draft". So there is no April 2026 mandate. There is no "regulatory floor" already live. The document's opening argument, its "Why Act Now" close, and its ₹61,000 Cr demand framing all rest on a superseded draft. This was already flagged. Prior work in this repo lists as an explicit st
questions: Is the April 2026 MoRTH ADAS mandate real or based on a draft notification?
When do the actual notified regulations like GSR 834(E) make AEBS and LDWS mandatory for commercial vehicles?
What are the binding dates for commercial vehicle ADAS compliance in India?

units.title: C2. The ₹1 Cr defence revenue is misdescribed four ways
units.body: The IM states "₹1Cr Defence Revenue" on the cover, "₹1 Cr institutional defence revenue RECEIVED Q1 2026" on p.15, "₹1Cr Defence Revenue Received" as a completed milestone on p.18, and "₹1 Cr defence revenue already received" in the exit vectors on p.26. Prior verified work finds: ₹23.01L delivered (GeM Robot Training); ₹78.39L is L1 — lowest bidder, not an award; it sits in Deepgrid Datacentre Pvt Ltd, not Deepgrid Semi; and IP on the delivered contract is MCEME-owned under Clause 27. The company's own BP-1A states "none of it is trucking/ADAS revenue." Four separate problems in one number: 78% of it is not revenue, it is in a different legal entity than the one raising, the IP does not belong to the company, and none of it is ADAS. A single diligence question retires it.
questions: What is the reality behind the claimed ₹1 Cr defence revenue?
Which legal entity actually holds the ₹78.39L L1 defence amount, and who owns the IP under Clause 27?
How much of the reported defence revenue has actually been delivered versus sitting as an L1 bid?

units.title: C3. The competitor set omits every threat that prior work ranked highest
units.body: The IM names Mobileye, Bosch, Steradian, Horizon Robotics, Nvidia, Netrasemi, NXP, Mindgrove, Aurora, Kodiak, ABB/Kalmar, ideaForge, Apptronik and Agility, and asserts on p.19 that Indian competition is a "genuine open lane… the one unit where 'no Indian competitor' is unambiguously true." Not named, and ranked as the real threats: - ZF WABCO — ADAS already shipping as OE fitment with a leading Indian CV OEM, with an in-house Indian test track and homologation capability DeepGrid concedes it lacks. Prior work calls this the actual threat, "not Nvidia/Mobileye." - Starkenn — company-reported 2,500+ vehicles and 30% of revenue from government tenders, plus BrakeSafe radar AEBS; highest threat in the government/mining segment the IM treats as open. - drivebuddyAI — $2.5M contracted across 3,000 heavy trucks (May 2026), scope to 10,000. No longer demo-only. - bitsensing — India retrofit ADAS kit launched Feb 2026 with an IKIO channel MoU. - Gahan AI, Aptiv, STRADVISION, Sterling Tools × MINIEYE. Netrasemi's ₹107 Cr Series A also demotes "India-native" as a differentiator — domestic origin alone no longer distinguishes DeepGrid.
questions: Why does the competitive landscape omit major threats like ZF WABCO, Starkenn, and drivebuddyAI?
Are there active Indian competitors or retrofit providers in the market that the IM ignores?
What real-world commercial traction do competitors like drivebuddyAI and bitsensing have in India?

units.title: C4. The import price column cannot be sourced, and quoting it was already banned
units.body: p.14 prices Mobileye at ₹5–8L, Continental ₹8–12L, Nvidia ₹12–18L, Qualcomm ₹10–15L, footnoted only as "public product specifications" with no citation. No public per-unit India price exists for Mobileye EyeQ6, Bosch/Continental, Qualcomm SA8295 or Nvidia Orin truck ADAS. Six of 27 rows in a prior evidence ledger are UNVERIFIED and all six are import prices; bitsensing's "pricing agreed case by case" corroborates that this is market structure, not a search failure — automotive ADAS unit pricing is quoted, not listed. A prior deck made quoting such a figure an explicit banned action. Stage 1 already showed the "3 to 7×" claim contradicts its own table (the range is 2.0×–9.0×). Loaded with NRE at plan volumes, prior work puts the real advantage at ~2.3×, and notes that the same category error — comparing a competitor ASP to DeepGrid's die cost — is what forced an earlier "774×" claim to be retracted.
questions: Where does the IM source its import pricing for competitors like Mobileye and Nvidia, and are those figures verifiable?
How does the actual cost advantage compare to the 3 to 7x multiplier claimed in the deck?

units.title: C5. The 88% gross margin is arithmetically unreachable
units.body: The IM projects 88% blended GM at FY2032. Prior analysis: 88.4% blended requires ~120% margin on all non-kit revenue. At 72% kit margin the honest blend is 77.2%. An 11-point GM error at FY2032 revenue of ₹1,388 Cr is roughly ₹150 Cr of gross profit, which flows straight to the ₹536.6 Cr EBITDA line the deck leads with.
questions: Is the projected 88% gross margin arithmetically possible by FY2032?
How much does the 11-point gross margin error impact the EBITDA projections?

units.title: IMPORTANT — would materially raise confidence
units.body: - I1. Founder's public cost figures contradict the IM. In March 2026 the founder told Business Standard, ET Manufacturing, TechGig and Communications Today that the FPGA chipset costs "around ₹35,000" and the post-tapeout target is "₹3,000 per chipset," with tapeout "around $3 million." The IM's p.20 uses ₹65,000 FPGA and ₹1,750 ASIC die. The FPGA figure is 1.86× the founder's public number. Any investor who searches will find the quote. - I2. The die-cost confusion was already resolved and the IM still has it wrong. Prior reconciliation: $30 = complete board BOM, $3.876 = die alone at 1M units, and ₹1,750 (~$20) matches neither. Stage 1 found four die figures in the IM; with p.20's ₹1,750 it is five. - I3. The raise has moved and the old number is on the record. Founder public: ₹25 Cr (~$3M) for tapeout and marketing. A prior document set carried ₹25 Cr and ₹45 Cr simultaneously. This IM asks $4.0–5.0M (~₹35–42 Cr). Not wrong, but it needs a reason. - I4. OEM design-in contradicts the company's own scored ICP work. The IM positions OEM design-in as "the platform prize · next." A scored, red-teamed ICP ranked Automobile OEM / Tier-1 fourth at 2.32 (46.4%) and deferred it, with the worst certifica
questions: Do the founder's public statements on chipset costs contradict the figures in the IM?
What are the discrepancies between the founder's public raise amount and the current IM asking price?
How does the die-cost in the IM reconcile with previous board BOM and die-only breakdowns?

units.title: NICE TO HAVE — will not change the decision
units.body: - N1. Assets the IM leaves out that would strengthen it: field trials on humanoids, AMRs and AGVs for seaports; TiE Hyderabad Top 50; HDFC Parivartan Top 10 of 600+ applicants with a ₹25 lakh grant; a completed 130nm validation tapeout at ~₹20 lakh. The IM includes the VLSI Top 8 and the 130nm tapeout but not the rest. - N2. Product naming. DGrid-SoC, DGS001 and DG-A100 have all been used publicly for what appears to be one line. The IM adds "DGrid Alpha Chipset" and "A100."
questions: What positive assets or grants like HDFC Parivartan does the IM leave out?
How consistent is the product naming across different company materials?

units.title: What the IM gets right
units.body: Worth stating, because it is not all bad and one item is a genuine improvement over later company material. - 39.3 TOPS is correctly labelled a derivation, not a measurement. The Artix-7 board ceilings near 1.8 TOPS, and a later July deck wrongly upgraded this figure to "measured." This June IM does not make that error. - The 130nm SkyWater validation tapeout is disclosed rather than omitted. - The MicroDC-A1 roadmap slide carries an explicit conceptual-product disclaimer. - The P&L is footnoted as management estimates, not independently audited.
questions: What parts of the IM are actually accurate, such as the TOPS derivation and tapeout disclosures?
Does the IM correctly label the 39.3 TOPS figure as a derivation rather than a measurement?

units.title: Recommended sequence before this document is sent
units.body: 1. Replace every April 2026 / GSR 184(E) reference with the G.S.R. 834(E) timetable, and rebuild the timing narrative around the ASIC as a margin event, not market entry. 2. Restate the defence revenue as ₹23.01L delivered plus ₹78.39L at L1, name the entity, and disclose the MCEME IP clause. 3. Fix the ₹1,128 vs ₹1,388 Cr cover error and the four other internal contradictions from Stage 1. 4. Delete the import price column or replace it with a loaded-cost bridge at equal scope. 5. Re-derive blended GM from kit margin and show the bridge. 6. Add ZF WABCO, Starkenn, drivebuddyAI and bitsensing to the competitive view.
questions: What changes must be made to the regulatory timeline before sending the document to investors?
How should the defence revenue and competitive landscape be corrected in the dossier?

units.title: Limitations
units.body: - Every GBrain and repo source here is prior work by this same engagement, not independent third-party verification. It is well-evidenced and gazette-checked, but it is our own file. - Only two claims were checked against sources outside this engagement in this run: the mandate timetable and the AIS-162 draft status. - The cap table, valuation, historical financials and runway remain unobtainable from any source available here — they are internal documents that do not exist in the IM. Stage 1 gaps 1, 2, 4, 5 and 6 are still open and no research closes them. - Competitor per-unit India pricing is not merely missing but structurally unavailable.
questions: Are we relying entirely on internal company files for our due diligence data?
Where is the independent third-party verification for these GBrain and repo sources?
Why are the cap table, valuation, and historical financials still completely missing from the available documents?

units.title: Verification

units.title: Financial strengths (must survive the rebuild)
units.body: - Revenue built from unit volume × price per named product — makes the top line testable against capacity, channel and market size. - Selling prices held flat for six years; all growth comes from volume. - FY2027 presented honestly as an investment year at −30% EBITDA margin. - EBITDA and net income both turn positive in FY2028 — a short path to self-funding reduces capital at risk. - Segment definitions stated explicitly, so the revenue split is auditable. - Overheads scale smoothly rather than stepping.

units.title: Not findings
units.body: - 197% revenue CAGR. Ambition is the asset at this stage, and the plan decomposes growth into units and prices — the correct test, which it passes. - Flat six-year pricing. Reads as conservative. It matters only in combination with F-03/F-05, because it forces the whole margin burden onto cost. - Rounding drift ≤ ₹0.01 Cr across several P&L identities — inside the plan's own precision.

units.title: 1. BLUF
units.body: The segmentation in v3 is presentationally strong but not yet evidentially bottom-up, and three fixable defects — one arithmetic, one disclosure, one margin-mechanism — will surface in the first serious diligence pass. units.title: 3. Tension
units.body: The model's own Reconciliation tab already documents that the June 2026 Information Memorandum, now in investors' hands, disagrees with it. Every week the current model circulates unreconciled, the number of counterparties holding two contradictory documents grows. Separately, the plan's nearest-term promise — EBITDA breakeven in FY2028 — rests on a 20-point gross-margin jump in a single year, and has only a 6.3-point cushion. That is the first thing an analyst stress-tests, and it is the claim closest to the money.

units.title: 4. Argument arc
units.body: 1. Context — v3 exists to segment a plan the company already believes in; company-level figures are unchanged by design. 2. Credit — the build is genuinely decomposed to units × ASP per product, which is better than most material at this stage. 3. Tension — but three defects are visible to any analyst in under an hour. 4. Proof A (arithmetic) — FY2028 net income contradicts the model's own EBT and tax lines, and understates the company's story. 5. Proof B (disclosure) — the IM and the model disagree in opposite directions on linked figures, so at least one was never re-derived. 6. Proof C (mechanism) — segment margins are identical to one decimal across three unrelated businesses; the mix defense is arithmetically unavailable (6% of the expansion), and the residual converts to a ₹27,500 kit BOM. 7. Implication — the fragile claim is near-term, not terminal: FY2028 breakeven, not FY2032 scale. 8. Action — a ranked fix list, sequenced by what each defect costs in diligence.

units.title: 6. Evidence map
units.body: Direct evidence (Verified — re-derived from the file): FY2028 net income break (₹2.29 Cr); segment totals vs P&L drift in FY30/FY31; identical per-segment margins; margin bridge 6%/94%; breakeven-GM cushions; FY2032 concentration; R&D-to-payroll ratio; absence of formulas, cash flow, uses of funds. Fair synthesis: the IM/model contradiction is documented in the workbook's own Reconciliation tab; characterizing it as disclosure exposure is synthesis. The ₹27,500 BOM is arithmetic; calling it implausible for compute + software + sensors is synthesis. Interpretation (Judgement — no external benchmark run): that 89% is unreachable for a bundled hardware kit; implied headcount at ₹25L loaded cost; that flat six-year ASPs understate price erosion. All are analyst opinion and must be labelled as such on the slide, not presented as benchmarked.

units.title: 4. Retired claims still live in the prior deck
units.body: The prior deck is not clean. It asserts, on slide 31: "12.9× COST ADVANTAGE vs. Mobileye $50 ASP (sourced)" This is on the retired list — it compares their ASP to our die cost. It must not be carried forward into any new deck. It also states "₹1 Cr already received" with its own red-team flag that the nature of the revenue is unconfirmed. Later work resolved this: ₹23.01 lakh delivered, ₹78.39 lakh is L1 (lowest bidder, not an award), sitting in Deepgrid Datacentre — a different legal entity — with customer-owned IP, and none of it trucking or ADAS revenue. The prior deck's figure is ~4× the real one. My playbook's slide 14 ("What we are not claiming") is the only artifact in the set that gets this right. It should be carried into any merged deck unchanged.

units.body: 1. Adopt the prior scorecard's ranking. Re-weight to roughly 50% Tactical Defense & Off-Highway/Port · 35% Fleet Retrofit · 15% OEM/Tier-1 relationship-building only. Do not resource OEM at 30%. 2. Keep my Decision 01, 04, the claim-hygiene slide, the gazette evidence and the qualification scorecard — these have no counterpart in the prior work. 3. Take their phase numbering, kill criteria, anti-ICP slide and red-team conditions. 4. Freeze all BOM figures until §3 is resolved. Three sources, three answers. 5. units.title: Sterling Tools partners MINIEYE to accelerate ADAS and Driver Monitoring Solutions for India
units.body: By Aman Shukla 4 min read·Published on Jan 19, 2026 · 6:25 AM IST·Updated Jul 14, 2026 · 12:37 PM IST Share on FacebookShare on XShare on LinkedInShare on WhatsAppShare by email Listen to this article Speed1.0x -Advertisement- Sterling Tools Limited (BSE: 530759 \ NSE: STERTOOLS), a leading automotive components and technology manufacturer, has partnered with MINIEYE, a China-based intelligent driving and in-cabin solutions provider listed on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange, to accelerate the deployment of Advanced Driver Assistance Systems and Driver Monitoring Systems tailored specifically for the Indian automotive market. The partnership is focused on adapting intelligent driving technologies to India’s unique and highly complex road environment. As part of the collaboration, Sterling Tools will support perception tuning and on-ground industry engagement, enabling ADAS and driver monitoring systems to be trained for India-specific road scenarios, mixed traffic conditions, and diverse driving patterns. This approach recognises that intelligent driving systems require deep data-driven perception development and application-level engineering to operate reliably in Indian conditions, rather than being direct replications of solutions deployed in global markets. units.title: The two branches, stated plainly
units.body: If Column B is viable: there is no Rs 20–35 Cr hole. Act 5 evaporates. PSU revenue becomes profit rather than a mortgage payment. Decisions (a) and (c) both need rewriting, and the company's identity shifts from "we own the die" to "we own India-tuned perception." That is a smaller story and a much shorter path to certified revenue. If Column B is not viable: the honest ICP for the next twelve months is a lead investor plus one NRE-funding Tier-1 partner. The sales organisation's job for that period is generating design-in evidence that closes the round — not booking PSU kit revenue. The playbook must be rewritten around that, and the 50/30/20 split is wrong as drawn. Both branches change the deck fundamentally. Neither is what the current 55 slides say.

units.title: Kill-criteria for the tapeout itself
units.body: The playbook contains four hard disqualifiers for customer deals and zero for the company's own Rs 25 Cr bet. That asymmetry is not serious. Adopt these, or write better ones: 1. Funding. If committed funding (equity + non-dilutive + Tier-1 NRE) has not reached the quoted tapeout cost by the tapeout decision date, do not tape out. 2. Anchor design-in. If no Tier-1 or OEM has signed an evaluation agreement naming the part before tapeout, the die ships into a market with no committed buyer. 3. Certification path. If AEC-Q100 and an ISO 26262 safety plan are not funded and scheduled, H1 2028 silicon cannot be line-fitted and the margin case cannot be realised. 4. Merchant-SoC parity. If a quoted merchant part reaches a 2027 ship date with qualification in hand and within an agreed cost delta of our die, the die is a luxury.

units.title: About ZF
units.body: ZF is a global technology company supplying advanced mobility products and systems for passenger cars, commercial vehicles and industrial technology. Its comprehensive product range is primarily aimed at vehicle manufacturers, mobility providers and start-up companies in the fields of transportation and mobility. units.title: ADAS unit pricing is quoted, not listedMETHOD
units.body: so the absence is structural — more searching will not produce a number BANNED FROM ANY SLIDE Any competitor per-unit price, in any currency, on any slide Any 'Nx cheaper than <competitor>' claim — it compares our die cost to their system price Any implied ASP derived from a contract value divided by a vehicle count State the cost argument as cannibalisation immunity — DeepGrid has no global ASP to defend, so it can price the India function at the India price.
